Next, select the sending network. 𝗜𝘁 𝗺𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗲𝘅𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝘄𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝘁 𝗼𝗿 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲. For example, to deposit $USDT through TRON, choose the TRON route marked TRC-20.
We’ll display the deposit address, QR code, current limits, and any required additional details.
𝗜𝗳 𝗮 𝗠𝗘𝗠𝗢, 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝗼𝗿 𝗗𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗧𝗮𝗴 𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗱, 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗱𝗱𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀. This code identifies the recipient when an address is shared by multiple users. The field name depends on the network and the sending service.
After scanning the QR code, check the additional field separately: the app may fill in only the address. If the sending service does not support the required code, use another sending method or another available route.
𝗔𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗺𝘂𝗺 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗮𝘅𝗶𝗺𝘂𝗺 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝗺𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝘀. Limits vary and may be updated, so check the current values for your selected route. If the sender deducts a fee from the transfer amount, account for the number of tokens that will actually arrive at the address.
𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗺𝘂𝗺, 𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗿, 𝗼𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁.

Send 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗹𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗿𝘆𝗽𝘁𝗼𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 from your external wallet. Before confirming, check the asset, network, address, additional code, and amount.

Once the transfer has been processed, we’ll credit the corresponding sg token to your balance. You can check the deposit status using 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁 and your transaction history.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗼 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗱𝘀
Once the deposit has been credited, open the relevant sg token in your asset list and select 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗺𝘂𝗺 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗺𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝘃𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗼𝗳 $𝟭𝟬𝟬 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘁. This threshold differs from the minimum deposit: you may be allowed to deposit a smaller amount into your wallet, but it will not be enough for staking.

Choose a staking period:
• 𝟯𝟬 𝗱𝗮𝘆𝘀
• 𝟵𝟬 𝗱𝗮𝘆𝘀
• 𝟭𝟴𝟬 𝗱𝗮𝘆𝘀
• 𝟯𝟲𝟬 𝗱𝗮𝘆𝘀

The plan displays the 𝗔𝗣𝗬 and the estimated reward at the end of the term. 𝗔𝗣𝗬 stands for annual percentage yield. It does not mean you receive the full annual percentage over one month or another selected period. To estimate your result, refer to the calculation shown in the plan.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗳𝗶𝘅𝗲𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗱𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗿𝘂𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘁. For example, staking sgXRP earns sgXRP, while staking sgUSDT earns sgUSDT. This principle applies to all the sg tokens listed above.

𝗘𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝘂𝗻𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮𝘃𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲. Staked funds cannot be transferred or withdrawn before the plan ends, so choose your amount and term according to your needs.

When the plan ends without renewal, we’ll return the staked tokens to your wallet and credit the reward. You can then use them within the available functionality.

If you want to use 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗹, enable the corresponding setting. Restaking is activated only if you choose it. Before confirming, check the term, reward calculation, and renewal setting.

Information about your active plan is available in the 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 section. For market-priced assets, the dollar value of both the staked amount and the reward may change even when the 𝗔𝗣𝗬 is fixed.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗼 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝗼𝗿 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗱𝗿𝗮𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗨𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗹𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝗿𝘆𝗽𝘁𝗼𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆

It’s important to choose the right operation.

With a regular transfer on the Stellar network, the recipient receives 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝘀𝗴 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻. Their wallet must support the corresponding asset.
To receive the underlying cryptocurrency on an external network, use 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗱𝗿𝗮𝘄. For example, to receive $XRP on XRP Ledger, withdraw sgXRP using this feature.
𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗱𝗿𝗮𝘄𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽𝘀:
Open the relevant sg token and select 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗱𝗿𝗮𝘄.

Choose an available receiving network.

Paste the recipient’s address and add a 𝗠𝗘𝗠𝗢, comment, or Tag if required.

Select 𝗡𝗲𝘅𝘁, enter the amount, and review the fee and limits.

Review the final details and confirm the withdrawal by selecting 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗿𝗺 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗱𝗿𝗮𝘄𝗮𝗹.

When sending to an exchange, use the details from its deposit section for the underlying cryptocurrency on the selected network. Use the recipient’s address and additional code, rather than the details we provided for funding your Sl8 wallet.

𝗙𝗲𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲. Before confirmation, the wallet will display the recipient’s details, the total amount to be deducted, and the number of tokens to be received. If you notice an error, return to the previous step and correct it.

Arrival time depends on transaction processing, the destination network, and the receiving service’s rules. When sending to an exchange, crediting also depends on the number of confirmations it requires.

𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗡𝗲𝘅𝘁?
We’re continuing to expand the available options:

• We’re working on Polygon support for sgUSDT and $USDT.
• We plan to add Arbitrum and Base for sgETH and $ETH.
• We’re preparing new assets: sgBTC 𝗳𝗼𝗿 $BTC 𝗮𝗻𝗱 sgHYPE 𝗳𝗼𝗿 $HYPE.

𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮𝘃𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘆𝗲𝘁. We’ll announce their launch and terms of use separately.

𝗜𝗳 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗡𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗛𝗲𝗹𝗽
If you have questions about funding your wallet, staking, transfers, or withdrawals, contact our support team. We’ll help you understand the issue and explain the next steps.
You can contact us directly in the Sl8 app: open 𝗦𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 and select 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁. You can also reach out through our Telegram group, 𝗦𝗹𝟴 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁  https://t.co/FBbgetI3ob .

If your question concerns a transfer, specify the asset you sent, the network you used, and the amount. Include the 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗿 - 𝗧𝘅𝗜𝗗, 𝗼𝗿 𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗵. This is the unique code for the transfer, which you can find in the transaction details in the sending wallet or exchange. These details will allow us to locate the transaction and check its status.

text:
The loops have been on my radar from years but didn't get to do them, yet. Your plan looks good but I would suggest to look at Cao Bang loop as an alternative to Hà Giang Loop. Ha Giang is very commercialised now. Also apply for IDP in advance and join a group. Cao Bang also includes ban gioc waterfall.

I love ninh Binh but 2 nights are enough.

Danang needs more days. Danang, Hoi An and Bana Hills each deserve 1 night each. Marble mountains and If you want, My Son Sanctuary, can be good additions. HCMC is ok for flight back 👍🏼

text:
Most people leave Ba Na Hills right when it starts becoming magical.

Big mistake.

Stay overnight. Trust me.

☁️ You take the cable car up… and halfway through, you’re literally inside the clouds. Everything goes silent. It doesn’t feel real.

🌙 And when everyone leaves?
Ba Na Hills turns into a ghost town (the good kind). Quiet, peaceful, surreal.

🌉 Next morning hits different — Golden Bridge, no crowds, just clouds flowing beneath your feet. Feels like you're walking in the sky.

Why overnight is a game-changer:
✨ Sunrise at Golden Bridge = 100x better than crowded daytime chaos
✨ French Village at night feels straight out of movie set.
✨ Cool weather + mist = unreal vibe all around
✨ Zero rush. You actually feel the place
✨ Early access before the tourist buses arrive

Ba Na Hills isn’t about ticking a box.

It’s about that one moment where you stop… and just take it all in.

text:
Who wants to visit this beautiful place??

This is the Golden Bridge (Cầu Vàng) in Vietnam 🇻🇳  

> located in Ba Na Hills near Da Nang  
> 150-meter-long bridge held by giant stone hands  
> sits around 1,400 meters above sea level  
> the hands are designed to look ancient and weathered  
> surrounded by clouds, mountains and crazy views  
> visitors reach it through a massive cable car ride  
> best time to visit is early morning before the crowds  
> ticket + cable car access costs around $40  
> one of the most viral travel spots in Asia right now  

The craziest part is those giant hands aren’t real stone… they’re actually built with steel and fiberglass

Would you actually walk on this bridge or nah?

Bana Hills: French Colonial Charm Meets Modern Amusement in Da Nang, Vietnam🌃💮🌼

Experience the enchanting Bana Hills in Da Nang, Vietnam  where a whimsical amusement park stands on the site of an early 20th-century French colonial village. Nestled in the mountains this unique destination offers a blend of historical architecture lush gardens, and thrilling rides. Highlights include the iconic Golden Bridge French-style castles and panoramic views of the surrounding landscape. Whether exploring the cultural replicas or enjoying the attractions Bana Hills promises a memorable adventure for all ages.💮💮

Vietnam 🇻🇳

Bana Hills in Da Nang is an amusement park built on the site of an early 20th century French colonial village. It’s worth visiting here for three reasons: ride the highest cable car in the world, walk along the Golden Bridge and see the French village.

Ba Na Hills is a very atmospheric place and a must visit in Da Nang. You can skip Marble Caves and Michonne, but not going to Ba Na Hills is a crime. In my opinion, Bana Hills Park is one of the best attractions in Vietnam.

text:
Golden Bridge, Hòa Phú, Vietnam 🇻🇳

This spectacular bridge supported by two gigantic hands looks like something out of a fantasy universe. 

The giant hands supporting the bridge symbolize something divine, mythical, or godlike. It does look as though they are lifting the bridge as a gift from the ground. 

The bridge’s principle architect, Vu Viet Anh, has even said that the goal of the design was to “invoke the sensation of walking along a thread stretching through the hands of God.”

📍Location: inside the Ba Na Hills resort near Da Nang in Vietnam

text:
Ba Na Hills – A Little Europe in the Heart of Vietnam (Central Vietnam)
Have you ever dreamed of visiting Europe while traveling in Vietnam? Ba Na Hills offers exactly that experience.
Perched high in the mountains near Da Nang, Ba Na Hills is one of Vietnam's most famous attractions. Its European-inspired architecture, cool mountain climate, and spectacular panoramic views have made it a favorite among international visitors.
The moment you arrive, you'll feel as though you've stepped into a charming European village surrounded by clouds and mountain scenery.
Highlights of Ba Na Hills include:
• Stunning French-style architecture.
• Beautiful mountain landscapes.
• Cool weather all year round.
• Spectacular cable car experiences.
• Iconic landmarks and unforgettable photo opportunities.
Best time to visit:
• March to August offers ideal weather conditions.
Whether you're traveling with family, friends, or your loved one, Ba Na Hills promises a magical experience unlike anywhere else in Vietnam.

quoted_tweet.text:
I had read so much about Ba Na Hills, Vietnam ... I guess I was expecting a bit too much.

While the place is definitely built beautifully, I was put-off by the crowds and a bit by the artificial-ness of the whole thing. 

When we arrived here, it felt like a crowded carnival with huge lines and bigger groups. Coming from India, I hate crowds and got a little put-off immediately.

Around 50% junta staying here are Indians, including us. Don't want to say much, but I did have to call the reception to get a group to stop shouting at the top of their voices in the corridors at 10 in the night.

The second thing is the amount of construction happening here. Cranes & unfinished buildings in many directions. Plus, no matter what they have done, it does feel artificial after the initial wow of the first hour or so.

And the biggest issue is that there is no guide or information available. You are left to roam around and figure it out on your own.

On the plus side, the food has been excellent. Wife has been pretty happy. It does quieten a bit in the evening, but still has a lot of people. The weather is awesome here!

text:
In the shadow of the Himalayas, Nepal doesn’t just build suspension bridges — it hangs them across one of the world’s deepest gorges so you can walk (or leap) above the abyss.

The star for pure engineering flex is the Gandaki Golden Bridge (Gandaki Sunaulo Jhula), a single-span steel suspension footbridge connecting Baglung and Parbat districts over the Kali Gandaki River. Opened in 2020, it stretches an uninterrupted 567 meters (1,860 ft) with no intermediate supports and hangs 122 meters (400 ft) above the river. At opening it was briefly the world’s longest single-span footbridge; it remains one of the longest in Asia and a top contender for dramatic length in mountainous terrain. Capacity: up to 612 people at once. It slashed a multi-hour slog of steep trails into a roughly 10-minute walk, linking communities that once detoured for hours or days.

Imagine stepping onto a narrow metal deck that sways gently 120–200+ meters above a raging Himalayan river, with snow peaks in the distance and nothing but air and cables between you and the canyon floor. No car, no guardrails that feel solid — just you, the wind, and the pure geometry of a suspension bridge doing its job in one of the planet’s most extreme landscapes.

text:
Christine Buckley was born in Dublin in 1946. But this baby girl had a Nigerian father which in 1940s Ireland was quite unusual. Christine was placed in Goldenbridge Industrial School in Inchicore, run by the Sisters of Mercy, and there she stayed until her teens.

Goldenbridge was meant to be a place of safety and care for kids. But like most Industrial Schools it was a prison for innocent children where they suffered hunger, beatings and fear. And any difference,  like being a mixed-race child, got you singled out for particular cruelty. Industrial Schools also involved forced child labour. In Goldenbridge girls were made to produce rosary beads in bulk, with punishment waiting for anyone who fell short of the quota. The irony of tarnishing a symbol of love and Gods mother by abusing children forced to manufacture them is a unique evil.

After surviving years of incarceration Christine finally was old enough to leave and trained as a nurse and midwife, and spent years bringing other people's babies safely into the world. Like countless other women failed by the state and church they made a career being kinder and more humane to the innocent. 

In 1992, Christine Buckley told her story (and in doing so the story of countless other victims) on The Late Late Show. And sadly, like so many other tales of injustice told before Irish society was able to accept it, the reaction against her was ferocious. She was doubted, attacked and accused of exaggeration. And some of the doubters were powerful and had obvious self interests. 

She kept going anyway. The 1996 documentary Dear Daughter put the stories of survivors in front of a national audience, and denial became far harder to sustain. In 1999 the State finally apologised, and the Ryan Report of 2009 confirmed what survivors had said for decades.

Christine Buckley founded the Aislinn Centre to support former residents of the institutions and gave hundreds of them something they had rarely had, a room full of people who believed them. She pressed for redress and for the truth to be told in full.

She was the recipient of the Irish 'Volunteer of the Year' award in 2009. In December 2012, Trinity College awarded her an honorary Doctor of Laws degree in recognition of her work for people who were subjected to institutional abuse. She passed away on 11 March 2014, aged 67, having forced a nation to face its past and also created a better future for girls and women in Ireland. 
https://t.co/oTif9EzntZ

text:
Day 4 | 16 June 2026

Ba Na Hills → Da Nang

Early Morning

Started the day early to experience Golden Bridge before the crowds arrived.

6:30 AM – Took the gondola to Golden Bridge.

Spent nearly two hours exploring the area around the bridge. While the Golden Bridge is the main attraction, there are several beautiful gardens, viewpoints and walking trails beyond the bridge that many visitors tend to miss.

Tip: Don’t just stop at the Golden Bridge. Walk further down and explore the surrounding attractions—you can easily spend a couple of hours here.

8:15 AM – Returned to Mercure Danang French Village Bana Hills.

⸻

Morning

Had breakfast at the hotel.

9:35 AM – Checked out of the room.

Spent the next few hours enjoying the attractions at Fantasy Park.

Highlights included:

Bumper Cars

text:
A couple of travel tips for visiting the Golden Bridge in Da Nang, Vietnam.

1. Take the Scenic Cable Car Ride: Access the bridge via the world's longest cable car system at Sun World Ba Na Hills (about 20-25 minutes from the base)—book tickets online in advance (around 950,000 VND/~$38 USD) to skip lines and enjoy stunning aerial views of misty mountains and forests en route.

2. Visit Early Morning or Late Afternoon: Arrive right at opening (7 AM) or toward sunset for fewer crowds, cooler temps (year-round average 15-25°C/59-77°F), and magical lighting over the 150m-long bridge held by giant stone hands—perfect for epic photos without the midday haze.

📍"The Golden Bridge, or Cầu Vàng", in Vietnam 🇻🇳 is a remarkable architectural piece located in the Bà Nà Hills resort near Da Nang.

The bridge stretches approximately 150 meters long and features a unique design with two giant stone-like hands lifting a golden thread of walkway. This design not only serves as an artistic statement but also as a functional pedestrian pathway.

First, the technical part, because it matters. Stellar has no proof-of-stake. Its consensus (SCP, a federated Byzantine agreement model) has no validator staking and no protocol inflation rewards.

So this isn't on-chain validator staking. It's a centralised, custodial yield product. You lock your assets with Cassator for a fixed term, and Cassator pays the rewards from its own platform, not the network.

Open Sl8 Social and activate your wallet or deposit an eligible asset (e.g. USDC) Go to Wallet > Staking and pick your term

text:
This is the Chapa Express, one of the most memorable experiences from my recent Vietnam trip. With its vintage-style interiors, private cabins and breathtaking views of the Vietnamese countryside, the train journey between Hanoi and Sapa feels truly regal.

And that's just one part of Vietnam's tourism appeal.

From the pristine beaches of Phu Quoc and the excitement of VinWonders and Vinpearl Safari to Da Nang's iconic Golden Bridge and the breathtaking landscapes of Ha Long Bay, Vietnam has established itself as a tourist hot favourite.

Why can't India do the same?

India has everything: mountains, beaches, forts, temples, wildlife and a rich cultural heritage. What we need is better infrastructure, cleanliness, reliable transport, tourist-friendly services and memorable experiences.

We don't lack attractions. We lack the ability to package and showcase them effectively.

What should India do to become a preferred international holiday destination?

text:
As a Vietnamese person, I truly feel ashamed and saddened when I witness the actions of some Vietnamese people that are damaging the image of our country in the eyes of Japanese people. Theft, breaking the law, dishonesty, and a lack of respect for the local culture and the shared rules of the society they live in are not things that should be taken lightly simply because the people responsible are our fellow countrymen.

I understand that the actions of a few people should not be used to judge an entire nation. Many Vietnamese people live, study, and work in Japan diligently and decently, always striving to build a positive image of their homeland. But that is precisely why wrongful behavior deserves to be condemned even more, because it can cause other innocent Vietnamese people to face suspicion and prejudice.

I sincerely apologize to the Japanese people who have unfortunately had bad experiences with Vietnamese individuals who have behaved unethically or broken the law. I know that an apology from one individual cannot replace the responsibility of those who committed the wrongdoing, but at the very least, I want to show that not all of us are indifferent to these issues.

text:
Every Language Tells a Story. Every Language Has a History.

Ever wondered how English, French, Spanish, Hindi and Persian are connected? Or why Malay, Indonesian, Vietnamese and Chinese sound so different?

Languages are like family trees. They evolve, branch out, borrow from one another and carry centuries of history, migration and culture.

The fascinating part is that languages that sound completely different today may share a common ancestor thousands of years ago.

Every time we learn a new language, we’re not just learning words. We’re discovering how humanity connects.

Different languages. One human story. 🌏

text:
A conversation in China. A lesson for India. 🇮🇳🤝🇨🇳

During my business visit to China, I met Mr. Wu, a 40-year-old professional whose journey left a lasting impression on me.

Coming from a middle-class family, he began his career as a technical engineer. Recognising that his skills could be put to better use in a different role, he moved into technical machinery sales.

His performance led to overseas marketing responsibilities, beginning with Vietnam. Over approximately 14 years, he progressed to become Global Head of Overseas Sales at a major Chinese packaging machinery company, serving markets across India, the United States, Africa and beyond.

What impressed me was not just his professional growth, but also his approach to business.

During our conversations, I observed his interactions with business associates from the United States and Canada. His relationships reflected the importance of trust, communication and consistency in international business.

Machines may win orders, but relationships build lasting partnerships.

His family story also reminded me of India. Despite different languages, food and traditions, the desire to care for parents, educate children and build a better future is familiar across many Asian families.

Mr. Wu has two children and believes that education will be crucial in preparing them for a future increasingly influenced by AI.

This brings me to an important question for India:

How many talented young Indians are waiting for the right opportunity to prove themselves?

Our entrepreneurs and business leaders can make a real difference by providing mentorship, practical training, meaningful responsibilities and exposure to global markets.

Those who have progressed in their careers have an opportunity to help the next generation progress too.

My travels through China and Japan have also reinforced another lesson: when we travel abroad for education, business, work or tourism, our conduct contributes to the impression we leave of India.

Professional integrity, respect for other cultures, thoughtful communication and responsible behaviour matter.

My takeaway from Mr. Wu’s story is simple:

Invest in education. Give young people opportunities. Build business relationships on trust. Represent India with dignity wherever you go.

India has enormous talent. Our responsibility is to help that talent find its opportunity.

What practical steps can Indian businesses take to prepare young people for a more AI-driven, globally connected world?

#Leadership #India #China #YouthEmpowerment #ArtificialIntelligence #Education #GlobalBusiness #Entrepreneurship

46% of Canada’s population is now 1st/2nd generation immigrants, a significant number from Third World countries. The top 20 home countries of Canada’s new permanent residents in 2024, based on IRCC data. 
Canada admitted about 483,000 new PRs that year:
1.  ⁠India — 127,320
2.  ⁠Philippines — 32,300
3.  ⁠China — 29,950
4.  ⁠Cameroon — 21,200
5.  ⁠Nigeria — 20,380
6.  ⁠Eritrea — 16,585
7.  ⁠Afghanistan — 12,280
8.  ⁠Pakistan — 11,940
9.  ⁠Iran — 11,150
10.  ⁠France — 9,940
11.  ⁠United States — 9,320
12.  ⁠Colombia — 8,850
13.  ⁠Algeria — 8,255
14.  ⁠Syria — 7,745
15.  ⁠Morocco — 7,630
16.  ⁠Ukraine — 6,780
17.  ⁠Vietnam — 6,710
18.  ⁠Mexico — 6,410
19.  ⁠Brazil — 5,985
20.  ⁠Somalia — 5,790

About 4.9% of Canada’s population is Muslim— roughly 1.78 million people, per the 2021 census, the most recent official count. That’s more than double the 2.0% share from 2001.  The 2026 Census data will not be available until early 2027, but outside of Quebec, Muslims outnumber French Canadians -  by a wide margin.  
According to the CBSA, As of Oct 21, 2024, there were nearly HALF A MILLION people in Canada's removal inventory who were subject to removal processes.
A large portion of them faced
"unenforceable" removal orders, were being monitored, or were awaiting refugee status decisions (or pending permanent resident status).  There are at least 80,000 expired visa holders who are “missing” - the government has no idea where they are.
Meanwhile, Canadians are spending approximately $4,000,000,000 annually on “refugee settlement costs” (housing, healthcare etc.), even those whose refugee claims have been rejected but remain in the country pending appeal (going through the entire process takes several years).
And Mark Carney wants to keep increasing immigration numbers.

#ULTIMATEUZBEK DIARIES DAY 2 – A LAZY MORNING AND AN AFTERNOON OF EXPLORATION 🇺🇿 🕌

Day 2 of our #UltimateUzbek tour was a gentle, unhurried day in Khiva that ended with a memorable sunset.

Our guests had a pleasant, lazy morning, strolling through the narrow alleys of Ichan Kala, Khiva’s walled inner city, in the lovely weather, shopping in the bazaars or relaxing in one of the town’s cafés.

In the afternoon, we gathered in the sunny courtyard of our madrasa hotel to learn about the many connections between India and Uzbekistan: stories of trade, scholars and travellers that bound our two lands together for centuries.

Then began our guided walk through the heart of the old city. We started at the Kunya Ark, the old citadel and residence of the Khans of Khiva, and went on to the magnificent Pakhlavan Mahmoud Mausoleum, the Juma Mosque with its forest of carved wooden pillars, the Ak (White) Mosque, and the Islam Khoja Madrasa, whose minaret is the tallest in Khiva. We ended at the Tosh Khovli Palace with its richly tiled courtyards.

At sunset, we climbed the fort walls and watched the setting sun spread its orange light across the domes and minarets of Khiva. It was a moment none of us will forget, and neither will we forget dinner on the terrace of the famous Terrassa restaurant, overlooking the illuminated old city.

On Day 3, we head to the fabled city of Bukhara.

The World's Three Major Airline Alliances: Star Alliance, SkyTeam, and oneworld

In today's aviation industry, no single airline can realistically serve every major city on Earth. To expand their global reach while reducing costs and improving customer convenience, airlines have formed powerful international partnerships known as airline alliances. Three alliances dominate global aviation: Star Alliance, SkyTeam, and oneworld. Together, they account for well over half of global airline traffic and connect thousands of destinations worldwide.

What Is an Airline Alliance?

An airline alliance is a cooperative arrangement among airlines that allows them to:

Coordinate schedules
Share airport facilities and lounges
Offer reciprocal frequent-flyer benefits
Sell seats on each other's flights through codeshare agreements
Provide seamless baggage transfers and ticketing

For travelers, this means one ticket can cover multiple airlines, baggage can be checked through to the final destination, and elite-status benefits can be recognized across many carriers.

Star Alliance
Founded

May 14, 1997

Star Alliance was created by:

Air Canada
Lufthansa
Scandinavian Airlines (SAS)
Thai Airways
United Airlines

It was the world's first global airline alliance and remains the largest today.

Major U.S. Carrier

United Airlines

Current Member Airlines (2026)
Aegean Airlines
Air Canada
Air China
Air India
Air New Zealand
ANA
Asiana Airlines
Austrian Airlines
Avianca
Brussels Airlines
Copa Airlines
Croatia Airlines
EgyptAir
Ethiopian Airlines
EVA Air
ITA Airways
LOT Polish Airlines
Lufthansa
Shenzhen Airlines
Singapore Airlines
South African Airways
SWISS
TAP Air Portugal
Thai Airways
Turkish Airlines
United Airlines

26 member airlines in total.

Network Characteristics

Star Alliance has exceptionally strong coverage in:

Europe
Asia-Pacific
Africa
North America

It is often regarded as the alliance with the broadest international network.

SkyTeam
Founded

June 22, 2000

Created by:

Delta Air Lines
Air France
Aeromexico
Korean Air

SkyTeam was formed as a competitor to Star Alliance and later grew into the second-largest alliance.

Major U.S. Carrier

Delta Air Lines

Current Member Airlines
Aerolíneas Argentinas
Aeromexico
Air Europa
Air France
China Airlines

Garuda Indonesia
Kenya Airways
KLM
Korean Air
Middle East Airlines
SAS
Saudia
TAROM
Vietnam Airlines
Virgin Atlantic
XiamenAir

18 member airlines.

Network Characteristics

SkyTeam is particularly strong:

Across the Atlantic
In Europe
Northeast Asia
Latin America

The Air France-KLM-Delta partnership is one of the most successful airline joint ventures in the world.

oneworld
Founded

February 1, 1999

Founded by:

American Airlines
British Airways
Cathay Pacific
Qantas
Canadian Airlines

oneworld was designed to bring together many of the world's premium and long-haul international carriers.

Major U.S. Carrier

American Airlines

Current Member Airlines
Alaska Airlines / Hawaiian Airlines
American Airlines
British Airways
Cathay Pacific
Fiji Airways
Finnair
Iberia
Japan Airlines
Malaysia Airlines
Oman Air
Qantas
Qatar Airways
Royal Air Maroc
Royal Jordanian
SriLankan Airlines

15 member airlines.

Network Characteristics

oneworld excels in:

Premium international travel
Trans-Pacific routes
Australia and Oceania
Middle East connections

The alliance benefits greatly from flagship carriers such as Qatar Airways, British Airways, Qantas, and Cathay Pacific.

Benefits for Airlines
Revenue Expansion

Airlines gain access to markets they could not economically serve themselves. United Airlines, for example, can sell itineraries deep into Europe through Lufthansa, while Lufthansa can sell journeys throughout the United States using United's domestic network.

Lower Costs

Members share:

Airport lounges
Ground services
Marketing efforts
Technology platforms
Purchasing agreements

These partnerships lower operating expenses.

Better Competitive Position

Alliances allow carriers to compete more effectively against rival airline groups while maintaining independent brands.

Benefits for Travelers
Frequent Flyer Reciprocity

Passengers can:

Earn miles on one airline
Redeem miles on another alliance member
Receive elite-status recognition throughout the alliance

For example, United MileagePlus members may earn and redeem miles on Lufthansa, ANA, Singapore Airlines, and other Star Alliance partners.

Worldwide Lounge Access

Elite members and premium-cabin travelers often gain access to hundreds of lounges across alliance networks.

Easier Global Travel

Passengers enjoy:

Single-ticket itineraries
Through-checked baggage
Coordinated schedules
Simplified rebooking when disruptions occur
Alliance Rankings by Passenger Traffic

Based on the latest widely reported alliance passenger figures:

Rank Alliance Annual Passengers1 Star Alliance ~762 million
2 SkyTeam ~624 million
3 oneworld ~490-535 million

Star Alliance remains the largest airline alliance in the world by passengers carried. SkyTeam is second, while oneworld ranks third.

Alliance Rankings by Revenue and Profitability

Precise alliance-wide profit figures are not publicly reported because each airline remains an independent company. However, industry analyses consistently place the alliances in approximately this order by combined revenue:

Rank Alliance Estimated Revenue Strength1 Star Alliance Highest
2 SkyTeam Second
3 oneworld Third

A recent analysis of airline financial data found that Star Alliance members collectively generate substantially more revenue than either rival alliance, while SkyTeam and oneworld operate at roughly similar revenue levels.

This ranking is largely driven by large member airlines such as:

United Airlines
Lufthansa Group
Air Canada
Singapore Airlines

all belonging to Star Alliance.

Domestic vs. International Focus
Star Alliance

Primarily International

Many members are traditional flag carriers whose networks center on intercontinental traffic:

Lufthansa
Turkish Airlines
Singapore Airlines
ANA
Air New Zealand
SWISS

Although United and Air Canada provide significant domestic feed, Star Alliance's strength is overwhelmingly global.

SkyTeam

Balanced International and Domestic

Delta's enormous domestic U.S. operation contributes millions of passengers annually, while Air France, KLM, Korean Air, and China Eastern provide extensive international service. The alliance maintains a fairly even mix of domestic and international traffic.

oneworld

Strong Premium International Orientation

While American Airlines provides a huge domestic network, many of the alliance's most influential members are long-haul international specialists:

Qatar Airways
British Airways
Cathay Pacific
Qantas
Japan Airlines

oneworld tends to attract a higher share of premium international travelers than the other alliances.

Final Assessment

If judged by sheer size, network reach, passenger traffic, and combined revenue, Star Alliance remains the global leader, serving more countries and carrying more travelers than any competing alliance.

SkyTeam occupies the middle position, benefiting from the powerful Delta-Air France-KLM-Korean Air network and a balanced mix of domestic and international traffic.

oneworld, though the smallest of the three, arguably has the strongest concentration of premium international carriers and is particularly appealing to long-haul business and luxury travelers through airlines such as British Airways, Qatar Airways, Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, and Qantas.

Together, these three alliances form the backbone of modern global aviation, enabling travelers to reach nearly every corner of the world using a single ticket, a single loyalty program, and a seamless travel experience.

Rather than contesting Tariq Nasheed's premise regarding Foundational Black American and our connection to this land, we should focus on refining our overarching narrative, recognizing that our primary strategic competition lies with other Asians, Arab, Hispanic, Hindu-Indians, Black / African foreigners. 

I vehemently reject the term African-American. Africans have a bad reputation across the world,  they can barely travel outside their continent. I'm an Antebellum-Black / Antebellum-Moor American (Historical) & Anglo-Black / Anglo-Moor American (Modern)

Who is an Antebellum-Black / Foundational-Black / Antebellum-Moor / Anglo-Black / Anglo-Moor American? (Endonyms)  

1. English Speaking - English is their first language, native language & mother tongue.  

2. They bear English/Western surnames.   

3. Mostly Protestant Christians, with Catholic, Hebrew & Muslim minority.   

4. Practice & major contributors to American and Western Culture.   

5. American citizens by War, Birthright & Sacrifice, not by Naturalization.   

6. No ties, citizenship or affiliation with any African Tribes, Nations or Nationalities outside the USA.   

7. They have various admixture of Black Native, Moor, African, European, Hispanic, & Asian Ancestry.   

8. Prior to the outbreak of the Civil War (1861), an overwhelming majority, approximately 95% percent, of the Antebellum-Black / Antebellum-Moor American population resided in the 16 Southern States: Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, Arkansas, Tennessee, Kentucky, & Missouri. 

 9. They are Descendants of Black Natives, Negro, Freedmen, Moor, Creole, Mulatto, Quadroon, Octoroon and Melungeon who existed or resided in the United States of America before the Civil War (1776 - 1861) or (1500 - 1861).  

10. The term Antebellum-Black / Antebellum-Moor American (Historical) is to differentiate from: Post-Bellum Black / African Americans whose families arrived in the USA several decades after the Civil War (1865) and before December 31, 1979 & Latter-Day Black / African Americans whose families arrived on or after January 1, 1980.

11. Referred to as the Western Moor / Antebellum-Moor / Anglo-Moor Americans (Modern) to distinguish from: Eastern / Arabic-Moors from Medieval North-West Africa and Spain (Al-Andalus) who were Arabic speaking, bear Arabic names, practice Arabic culture and adhere strictly to Islamic Religious principles and laws.  

12. Participated in all American Wars, including the Revolutionary War, the First Barbary War, the War of 1812, the Second Barbary War, the Mexican-American War, the American-Indian Wars, the American Civil War, the Spanish-American War, World War I, World War II, the Korean War, the Vietnam War, & the Gulf Wars.

13. No group is more deeply rooted in American soil, more patriotic, or more invested in the nation's destiny than Foundational Black / Antebellum-Black / Antebellum-Moors / Anglo-Black / Anglo Moor Americans. Our loyalty is absolute; If the USA were to fall, we would remain here, fighting tirelessly to keep the American spirit alive, to preserve its existence.

text:
Japan Visa 📢

Here's to everyone who is about to apply Japan visa or just want to know about the Japan visa. You are in for a lot of good and legit information.

I have been following the Japan visa since good 2 years now and finally I have almost completed my research to write about it. Let me share what I have learned in years in few lines. 

Difficulty level- Easy but occasionally they refuse people randomly, at the same time "easy" isn't like Vietnam or Singapore easy. Don't be overconfident and they do reject visas. 

Documents required:- 

This can be variable, for example here's the snippet from Delhi, they stick to it unless your overall profile has some discrepancies etc. 

They can easily process your visa without any bank statements,  VFS representative removed my bank statements but I insisted to let it be. 

There's no job NOC requirement,  dummy tickets are accepted, also as a pro-active step attach 26AS
 
Cover letter is optional

Plus they are extremely extremely strict about jurisdiction and if you are from Gurgaon, I would still recommend to go to Delhi and apply from there as in Gurgaon they need demand draft for payment and are pretty slow, while in Delhi it's breeze and cash is accepted (no cards) 

I gave a photograph, which I had my Schengen visa application done some 2 years ago. 

Longer Validity 

Now this is something interesting, Japan Embassy randomly hands out 5 years visa and this is where my research was focussed on, many consultants/agents may promise you that we can get you  one and so one but can they? Short answer no. In depth analysis to follow. 

My experience 

I always get asked by friends family,  how do I travel in such a good budget,  people traveling in India pay more and hence I arranged a group tour for my family and friends where I am taking them to Japan and Korea for 2 weeks, the total cost of the trip came around 70k/person. All flights, stays included, no hostels. Either Airbnb or an Apartment. Visa costs are additional and I am helping all the group members with visa. 

I just received my Japanese visa and it took exactly 3 working days. 

Vfs was very smooth this time, no appointment needed. Total fees paid 1200 with passport self pick up. I had prepaid and booked everything in advance. I don't do dummy. 

Now did I try longer validity ? Yes! I did but still didn't get it. 

WARNING ⚠️:- DO NOT PLAN YOUR TRIP FOR MORE THAN 15 DAYS, they as a standard practice issue single entry 15 days and may request multiple/longer but is very discretionary. I know many applicants who lost a lot of money due to this. 

Now I have a travel history to all the G7 countries(they focus on this), permanent residenship in one of the G7, my bank statements were top notch, mutliple sources of Income and my job is also well paid with a top MNC, ITR was also solid and I travel a LOT. My passport is full of stamps and infact I could have applied an evisa from home and as a standard got a longer validity but even with this, Japan issued me a single entry 15 days 😅😅 

I have now sampled enough to tell you the 5 year visa is absolutely random, as I know a blank passport holder who didn't even give a cover letter get one 😅😅 will update on how it goes for remaining group members. 

Meanwhile if you have any questions, feel free to ask in the comments. Yes Japan visa for self employed may pose more documentation and care. 

PS- We would now be launching the Japan visa support at viszapp for those who need it.

text:
Planning your first International Trip on a Budget

- Every ₹ matters so choose a country with VOA + No or Less Visa Fee 
- The max cost on every trip is the flight and stay cost 
- Choose countries which have cheap flights and a good hostel network
- Backpacking is not for all I understand but it can save a lot of costs on flights from India and Internal too
- Starting with some easy to enter countries helps keep the cost of mistakes also to the minimum. You will learn a lot of things on the first trip which you will correct from the next one 
- Start off with Thailand, Vietnam or Sri Lanka depending on your choice and what you plan to do etc. 
- If hesitant to stay at an hostel but want to try to book a Mixed Dorm and can try living it for a day. Or a girls only dorm for safety etc. If it clicks, you can stay more days or else move to a hotel. 
- Plan your trip but also keep room for changes. While in SE Asia change of plans would not cost much, and you can do it as per your liking.
- Travel light. Those Instagram photos with different clothes can wait. Again if the photos bring you joy then please carry bags. Point here has been when you're traveling light you will slowly know what you would prefer, etc, and to make changes will be easier. From next trip onward you're better prepared. 
- Change cities. Change countries. Each city and country is different so explore more to know what you enjoy. 

#DakuKaGyaan

text:
The Health Ministry is trying to calm a public outcry over a bill that would, for the first time, let minors become tissue and organ donors in limited cases. 

In an Oct. 23 statement, the ministry said the draft “does not encourage donation by children.” It said the bill would still ban taking kidneys, livers, hearts, or other organs from living children and would allow donation after death only with a guardian’s consent. 

But the statement left out the issue that set off the backlash in the first place: a government survey that asked schoolchildren for their names and ethnicity, set a target of “100% of children” taking part, and never asked the parents. 

“How much can a 7-year-old understand?” one father asked on Threads, in a post that drew thousands of likes.

Read more: https://t.co/MdzLU1VpxE

text:
The Phong Nhị Massacre — Vietnamese Civilians Killed by South Korea’s Blue Dragon Brigade

On 12 February 1968, South Korean marines came under sniper fire in or near Phong Nhị, central Vietnam. One soldier was wounded.

The Blue Dragon Brigade’s 1st Company, 1st Battalion was operating in the village.

Nguyễn Thị Thanh was a child. Soldiers shot her in the abdomen. Her older brother was badly wounded. Their mother, older sister and younger brother were killed.

She survived multiple operations and about eight months in hospital.

In Phong Nhị and neighbouring Phong Nhất, 74 villagers were killed.

A U.S. report the following month described Phong Nhị as retaliatory killing after Korean troops received fire. It did not establish the full chain of orders. The sniper fire did not prove the civilians were responsible.

U.S. personnel helped the wounded, photographed the aftermath and investigated.

In 2020, Thanh sued South Korea. The government disputed its troops’ responsibility and argued that her claim was too late.

She won in February 2023. An appellate panel upheld the compensation ruling in January 2025.

As a Korean, I could have avoided this subject. But I could not look away.

Speaking for myself, I offer my heartfelt apology to the victims and survivors of these massacres, and their families.

What should acknowledging this massacre require beyond a court judgment?

text:
I didn’t start group trips as a business idea. There was no vision board. No five-year plan. They were just...trips I’d take anyway, and thought, why not take a few people along who’d enjoy them as much as I would.

One of the first was an all-women South Korea trip. Somewhere in the middle of planning it, an acquaintance joined in. Not just to join the trip, but to build it together. Same enthusiasm. Same work ethic. Same love for travel. We planned, we executed, and it worked. 

Naturally, we assumed this was destiny.

We planned more trips. Announced a few. Watched them not take off. Some were too offbeat. Some were victims of political unrest, or the Indian calendar’s deep attachment to weddings. 

Just repeated reminders that the market does not care about your excitement.

Then, Vietnam clicked. Affordable. Familiar. Required just enough leaves to not invite parental concern. 

And that’s when my business partner left.

"Group trips don't solve my purpose." She was done. Seven people had already paid.

That sentence did a lot of damage for something so short.

I considered cancelling the trip. Returning the money. Walking away with what little dignity I thought I had left. Not because I couldn’t do it alone, but because I suddenly felt like I’d misunderstood everything. The partnership. The plan. Myself.

I cried to my friends. And they said some annoying things to me:

Who else should take people to Vietnam?
You backpacked there in 2015. When Indians didn't know of the region! 
Vietnam is literally your home ground.
You've been inspiring us to travel before the word influencer marketing was coined!

Annoyingly accurate things. (love you all, you know who you are) 

So I went. The trip wasn’t perfect. Nothing ever is. But people laughed. They ate well. They felt safe. They gave feedback. Some of them are coming back for another trip, which still feels surreal. 

And then, recently, I saw that the same person who said group trips didn’t serve her purpose is now taking one. To South Korea.

I felt the things you’re supposed to feel. Anger and disappointment. I replayed conversations in my head like a terrible podcast I couldn’t unsubscribe from. I compared. I sulked. I did all the very human things you do when something ends badly.

Then, I felt relief.

Because I didn’t quit when it hurt.
I didn’t abandon the thing I loved just because someone else walked away. I didn’t turn joy into ego or scale or a pitch.

I didn’t start group trips to build a legacy or impress strangers on the internet. I started them because travel made sense to me long before growth charts did.

Somewhere in all of this, I found the real point. Not letting the hurt take the wheel. 

If you stuck till the end, I hope you find your point too. Also,  thank you for indulging my feelings. It was a long post! :)

text:
In 2020, a land dispute in the village of Đồng Tâm, outside Hà Nội, ended with thousands of police storming the village before dawn. An 84-year-old village elder was shot dead in his home, three officers died, and two of his sons were later sentenced to death. 

Six years on, as residents of Ba Vì fight Sun Group’s safari park, many Vietnamese on Threads are drawing the comparison. “Đồng Tâm version 2 is coming,” one user wrote. 

Others posted photos of the slain elder, Lê Đình Kình, and asked why villagers must now “kneel and beg for their own land.” 

Some of these posts have since been deleted, and pro-government accounts have flooded the comments calling them “subversive.” 

The comparisons come as authorities push to clear Ba Vì’s land by Dec. 8, despite weeks of protests and warnings from police against gathering.

text:
✈️ Vietnam Trip – Part 1
Starting off with the flight experience on Vietnam Airlines, which was mixed.

Departure: Mumbai to Hanoi
Check-in at BOM was smooth. Dedicated counter, helpful porter, actual fast-track. We felt like travel royalty-until we met the aircraft. Let’s call her "well-traveled." Lie-flat seats? ✅ 
Solid entertainment? ✅  
But the Indian vegetarian meal? Someone sent it on a silent retreat. Bland to the point of existential crisis. Mumbai catering, you had one job.

Return: Hanoi to Mumbai
Same airline. Same seat. Same Indian vegetarian meal. But this one had flavor, spices, even intent. It tasted like someone’s mom packed it with love.

Verdict?
💺 Seats: Worn but comfy  
🍽️ Food: Plot twist between legs  
💸 Value: Absolutely worth it (Flying Blue FTW)  
🎟️ Regrets: None (ok maybe some salt packets)

It wasn’t five-star all the way, but when you’re flying business on less cash, the highs hit higher and the lows feel like punchlines.

🪧 Coming up in Part 2: 3N in Hanoi

text:
No foreign tourist is willing to travel to India. 

It is dying slowly. 

Let's take an example of Goa. 

From 9.37 lakh foreign tourists in 2019 to only 4.67 lakh tourists in 2023.    

It has become too expensive for a common traveller to visit Goa.    

The opening of other avenues in Southeast Asia, like Vietnam and Indonesia, has also hit Goa's tourism.

You don't have to visit far; you can go to countries like Bali or Vietnam to notice the difference.  

Be it:  
- Cleaner public spaces. 
- Stronger hygiene of street food. 
- Stricter plastic control measures. 
- Cleaner environment with amazing AQi air. 
- Women's safety at night.  

No country is perfect, but India is struggling to give very basic things to its citizens.  

India can also become like them, even better. India has everything already. History, spirituality, food, art. Colour, Culture and People are amazing here.

Still, we are struggling to attract foreign tourists in India.

text:
In Ba Vì, on the outskirts of Hà Nội, residents fighting Sun Group’s planned safari park caught a car full of strangers measuring their gardens and fields on Oct. 27. 

When residents spotted it, the car sped off and hit three people, breaking one person’s leg, according to villagers who livestreamed what happened. Crowds surrounded the car and handed the people inside over to police. 

The next morning, according to a local livestreamer, the four people in the car had been released, while the officers questioned only the injured. Residents suspect the car was working for Sun Group, though that hasn’t been confirmed. 

The company hasn’t responded to questions, and neither local officials nor state media have said a word. For villagers who spent nights in September guarding their land against a secret groundbreaking ceremony, the incident felt like more of the same.

Read more: https://t.co/NsAgl5DCOQ

text:
Nearly a tonne of muscle. Horns like curved blades. And fewer of them left on Earth than seats in a single big-league stadium.

Your brain is about to file it under "cow." Don't.

This is the gaur. Bos gaurus. The largest wild cattle species on the planet, and one of the least discussed giants alive today.

Most people scroll past it. Most people have never even heard the name.

By the end of this post, you will not be able to look at the video above the same way.

Let's go.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE NUMBERS THAT DON'T FIT TOGETHER

Adult bulls weigh roughly 700 to 1,000 kilograms. The biggest ones have been credited with more. That's 1,500 to 2,200 pounds. That's a small car, wearing a leather coat, with a pulse.
Shoulder height: up to about 2.2 meters. That's over 7 feet at the shoulder. Taller than most grown men standing on their toes.
Body length: roughly 2.5 to 3.6 meters, tail not included.

Horns: up to around 80 centimeters of curved, pale-tipped, rock-hard keratin over a bone core.

Now here's the strange part.

An animal that size should be loud. Clumsy. Obvious. Something you hear coming for a mile.

And yet people who spend their lives in the forests of India and Southeast Asia will tell you the same thing again and again: you often don't see a gaur until you are already too close to it.

A tonne. Invisible.

How?

Hold that question. We'll come back to it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

IT IS NOT A BISON. IT NEVER WAS.

You'll see it called the "Indian bison" in older books and in plenty of tourist brochures.

That name is wrong.

Bison belong to the genus Bison. The gaur belongs to the genus Bos, the same genus as the domestic cow, the zebu, and the yak's closer relatives. It is wild cattle in the most literal sense.

The name "gaur" itself comes from Hindi. It has been used on the subcontinent for centuries.

Why does this matter?

Because a label shapes how much you care. "Indian bison" sounds like a copy of something famous. "Gaur" is its own thing. An original. And originals are worth protecting.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE BODY IS AN ENGINEERING ARGUMENT

Look at the silhouette of a gaur and your eye lands on one feature first: the ridge.

Along the shoulders and upper back, the animal carries a pronounced hump-like crest of muscle and bone. It slopes down toward the middle of the back, which gives the whole body a wedge shape, heavy at the front, lighter behind.

That ridge is not decoration.

The vertebrae in that region have long upward-pointing spines. Those spines are anchor points. They carry the enormous muscles and ligaments that hold up a head and a pair of horns that together weigh as much as a full-grown man's torso.

Think about what that means mechanically.

A head, carried at the end of a lever, in front of the body's center of gravity, swinging a pair of curved horns. Every degree of movement multiplies the load on the neck. Evolution solved this the way a civil engineer would: put the biggest structural support right where the biggest force lands.

Then look lower.

The legs of an adult are pale, almost stocking-white from the knee down, in strong contrast to the near-black body above. The dark body can look glossy, with a sheen that shifts to deep brown or blue-black depending on the light. Older bulls tend to darken further.

The contrast is not just pretty. Pale lower legs break up the animal's outline in tall grass and dappled light. In a forest of vertical stems and shadows, that matters.

Camouflage, on an animal the size of a van.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

SIZE IS A PROBLEM. THE GAUR SOLVED IT.

Here is something most people never think about.

Being big is hard.

Physics punishes giants in three ways.

First, the square-cube law. When an animal doubles in length, its mass grows roughly eight times, but the cross-section of its bones and muscles grows only about four times. Strength lags behind weight. Giants have to build thicker legs, denser bone, and sturdier joints, or they break.

Second, heat. A big body produces a lot of heat and has relatively little skin to shed it through. A mouse loses heat fast. A one-tonne animal in a tropical forest is basically a furnace that can't easily switch off.

Third, fuel. A big body needs a big amount of food, every single day, without exception.

Now look at how the gaur lives and you can see the solutions.

It tends to be most active in the cooler hours: early morning and late afternoon into dusk. Midday is for shade and rest. It uses water and mud to dump heat. It lives in hilly, forested country where shade is never far away.

Nothing about this is accidental. Every habit is a patch on a physics problem.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE FUEL BILL

An adult gaur needs to eat a staggering amount.

Cattle-sized herbivores typically need a few percent of their body weight in dry food every day. For a gaur, that points to something on the order of 20 kilograms or more of dry matter, which is far more in fresh grass and leaves.

That is not a snack. That is a full-time job.

It grazes on grasses. It browses leaves, shoots, and bamboo. It eats fruit when it can. It strips bark. And it seeks out natural mineral licks, spots in the earth where salts and minerals are exposed, because a plant diet alone does not always supply everything a body this big needs.

Notice what that really means.

Every day, a gaur has to find enough food to power a small car's worth of muscle, in a forest that is shrinking, shared with people, farms, roads and livestock.

Now you understand why habitat is not a "nice to have" for this species.

Habitat is the entire engine.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

WHY A TIGER THINKS TWICE

The tiger is the great predator of the same forests. It is also one of the few animals capable of killing a gaur.

But look at what the research and the field reports describe.

Tigers do take gaur. In some Indian reserves, gaur make up a major share of what tigers eat. But the pattern is consistent: tigers go for calves, young animals, and weakened individuals. A healthy adult bull is a very different proposition.

Here is the math from the tiger's side.

Tiger: up to around 200 to 250 kilograms. Healthy adult gaur bull: three to four times that, with horns, hooves, and the muscle to use them.

There are reports from the field of tigers being injured or killed by gaur. Predators know that every attack is a gamble where the downside is not a missed meal. It's a fatal injury, in a body that has to hunt every few days to stay alive.

This is the quiet logic of the whole food web.
Size is a weapon, yes. But size is also a contract. It says to everything around it: not me.

And the herd makes that contract stronger. Gaur usually live in small groups, often around eight to a dozen animals, led by an experienced older female. Adult bulls tend to roam alone or with small groups outside the breeding season. When a threat appears, the young are kept in the middle.

That is not an animal that survives by luck.

That is an animal designed by a very long argument with death.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

BACK TO THE QUESTION: HOW DOES A TONNE DISAPPEAR?

Remember the puzzle from the start?

Here's the answer, and it has three layers.

Layer one: color. A dark, matte-to-glossy body against shadow and foliage reads as just another patch of forest gloom. At dawn and dusk, when the animal is most active, that's exactly the light it lives in.

Layer two: behavior. Gaur are described as wary and, in places where they are hunted, strongly shy of people. A big animal that has learned to be quiet is a different creature from a big animal that doesn't care.

Layer three: the ground itself. Large hooves, wide spread of weight, a slow deliberate walk. Heavy does not have to mean noisy. A deer-sized animal crashing through brush makes more racket than a calm giant that knows where it's going.

Put those together and you get something almost absurd.

An animal that can weigh over 900 kilograms and still slip out of sight in a few steps.

If that doesn't make you want to look again, nothing will.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

A HISTORY OF GIANTS

Zoom out. Way out.

For most of the last two million years, the world was full of enormous land animals. Mammoths. Giant ground sloths. Enormous wild cattle. Rhinos with coats. Elephants on nearly every continent.

Then, over the last roughly 50,000 years, most of the largest land mammals on Earth vanished. The causes are still argued about: climate change, human hunting, or a mix of both. What nobody argues about is the result.

The giants went away.

Some regions kept more of them than others. Africa and southern Asia held on to much of their large-animal life. That's why you can still find elephants, rhinos, buffalo, tigers, and gaur sharing the same landscapes in parts of Asia today.

In scientific shorthand, a "megaherbivore" is an animal over about 1,000 kilograms. The biggest gaur bulls sit right at that line.

So when you look at a gaur, you're not only looking at a cow-like animal.

You're looking at a survivor from an older world. One of the last living echoes of a time when the forests belonged to giants.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

GIANTS BUILD THE LANDSCAPE

Here is where it gets interesting, and where most people stop reading.

Big herbivores are not just residents of an ecosystem. They are its architects.

A herd of large grazers does several things at once.

It opens up the vegetation. Grazing and trampling keep grass short, which changes how sunlight hits the ground, which changes which plants grow.

It moves seeds. Fruit eaten in one place is deposited, with its own fertilizer, a long way away.

It feeds the soil. Dung is not waste. It's the nutrient delivery system of the whole forest floor, and it supports insects, fungi, and birds in a long chain.

It makes trails. Paths worn through dense forest are used by smaller animals for years.

It shapes the fire risk. Less dry grass means less fuel.

Take the giants out and the whole structure changes. Often slowly, often invisibly, and often in ways that take decades to measure.

This is why conservationists talk about "keystone" and "ecosystem engineer" species.

The gaur may not be talked about as loudly as the tiger or the elephant. But it's doing a version of the same job, every day, while almost nobody watches.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE SLOW MATH OF A GIANT LIFE

Big animals live on a different clock.

A gaur cow carries a single calf, for roughly nine months. Not litters. One. One calf, many months of dependence, a long road to adulthood.

Compare that with a rabbit. Or a rat. Or a deer that can give birth more often.

Slow reproduction is the hidden weakness of every giant.

When a population of small animals is hit, it can bounce back fast. Three litters. Five litters. Done.

When a population of giants is hit, the recovery is measured in decades.

That's the part that makes every single loss count more.

Lose a breeding female and you haven't lost one animal. You've lost all the calves she would have raised over the next ten or fifteen years.

This is the arithmetic that has quietly been working against the species.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE NUMBER THAT SHOULD BOTHER YOU

The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists the gaur as Vulnerable.

The most-cited estimates for mature individuals fall somewhere in the range of roughly 13,000 to 30,000 animals across the whole of its range. And that range is not one clean block of forest. It is a scatter of patches, spread across India, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia.

The species is considered to have declined substantially across much of its range over the last few decades. It has already been lost from some places where it once lived, including Sri Lanka.

Let that sink in.

Total world population, by the optimistic count: less than a third of a single football stadium crowd.

Spread across nine countries.

Broken into islands.

And that's for an animal that can weigh nearly a tonne and fear almost nothing in its forest.

It tells you something uncomfortable.

Size does not protect you from us.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

WHAT ACTUALLY KILLS A GIANT

Not predators. Not the dry season. Not old age.

Three things, mostly.

One: habitat loss. Forests cut, converted to farms, roads, plantations, and reservoirs. A gaur's home range has to contain food, water, shade, and mineral licks. Chop the range into islands and the herd has nowhere to go.

Two: hunting. In many parts of its range, gaur are hunted for meat, and in some places for trophies or traditional uses. Even low levels of hunting, on a slow-breeding species, add up faster than people expect.

Three: disease. Gaur are cattle. They catch cattle diseases. In the past, epidemics such as rinderpest, spread from domestic livestock, wiped out huge numbers of wild cattle and related wildlife across Asia and Africa. Rinderpest was declared globally eradicated in 2011, one of only two diseases ever wiped out on purpose. But foot-and-mouth disease and other livestock illnesses remain a real threat when wild herds share grazing land with domestic cattle.

Look at that list.

Not one of them is a story of a stronger animal beating the gaur.

Every one of them is a story about what we built around it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE TIME WE TRIED TO CLONE ONE

In January 2001, a calf was born in Iowa.

Its mother was an ordinary domestic cow.

Its genetic parent was a gaur.

The calf was named Noah. He was the first cloned animal of an endangered species. Scientists had taken cells from a gaur, placed the genetic material into an egg from a domestic cow, and brought the pregnancy to term in a cow that was not even the same species.

It was a headline for about a week.

Noah lived for roughly two days. He died of a common infection, a dysentery-type illness that researchers said was not tied to the cloning itself.

Think about the symbolism for a second.

We can copy the genome of a giant. We can persuade a different species to carry it. We can do it with lab equipment that fits on a table.

And we still can't reliably keep wild herds alive in a forest.

That's not a failure of science.

That's a statement about priorities.

Technology is excellent at producing a single miracle. It is terrible at doing the boring, expensive, unglamorous work of protecting a place.

A cloned calf makes the news.

A protected corridor of forest doesn't. But it's the corridor that actually keeps a species alive.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE DOMESTIC COUSIN NOBODY TALKS ABOUT

Here's another twist.

In the hills of northeastern India and neighboring regions, there's a semi-domesticated bovine called the mithun, or gayal. It's a large, heavily built animal, and it's closely related to the gaur. Many researchers consider it either a domesticated form of the gaur or a gaur-cattle hybrid lineage. The exact origin is still debated.

Whichever it is, it points to an old and surprising relationship.

People have lived alongside this family of animals for a very long time. In some communities the mithun carries real cultural weight. It features in rituals, in status, in social life.

So the wild form is not an alien. It's a long-lost neighbor.

And that makes its decline stranger.

We took the tamed version into our homes and our traditions.

And we let the original slip out of the forest.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

WHY THE BIG ONES ARE THE HARDEST TO SAVE

There is a cruel pattern in conservation.

The bigger the animal, the more space it needs. The more space it needs, the more it collides with us. The more it collides with us, the less we tolerate it.

A gaur does not need much from humans. It just needs to be left alone, with enough forest to move through.

But a hungry herd near a village crop is a conflict. A gaur wandering onto a road is a hazard. A large animal that shows up in a plantation or on the edge of a town makes news, and rarely good news.

Think of what coexistence actually demands.

Land set aside that produces no immediate income. Corridors that connect one forest to another. Compensation for farmers who lose crops, so that anger doesn't turn into poison or a snare. Rangers who are paid and equipped. Local communities who benefit from the animals being alive.

None of that is glamorous.

All of it works.

The places where gaur populations are stable or recovering almost always have the same ingredients: strong protection, genuine enforcement, and people who gain more from a living forest than a cleared one.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WHAT A CAMERA TRAP KNOWS THAT YOU DON'T
Scientists track animals like this with remote cameras strapped to trees.
They trigger on heat and motion. They work day and night, in monsoon and drought. And they keep producing footage of animals that behave very differently when they believe nobody is watching.

A big herbivore in an unobserved forest is calm. Methodical. It has routes it has walked for years. It knows where the water is, and when.

That's the thing about wildlife footage that gets lost in the era of the fast scroll.

You are not seeing a performance.

You are seeing an animal going about its business in a system it has been tuned to for hundreds of thousands of years.

The slowness is the point.

The patience is the point.

The sheer calm of something that doesn't need to prove it is dangerous, because everything around it already knows.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE ONLY QUESTION THAT MATTERS

We live in an odd moment.

We can build machines that write essays, model proteins, and generate video of things that never existed.

We can put a camera in your pocket that sees better than any eye in nature.

And meanwhile, a creature that weighs nearly as much as a small car, that has survived for hundreds of thousands of years, that sits in the middle of an ecosystem holding it together, is quietly running out of forest.

Not because it's weak.

Because nobody was looking.

That's the entire problem, stated as plainly as it can be.

Extinction does not announce itself. It doesn't arrive with a siren. It arrives as a quiet drop in a number nobody was checking, in a forest nobody was visiting, in a species nobody could name.

Attention is the first form of protection.

Which is why a short clip of a gaur, moving through its habitat at its own pace, is not a throwaway piece of content.

It's evidence.

It's a record that this animal is still here, right now, in your lifetime, in your generation, doing what it has always done.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THREE THINGS YOU CAN ACTUALLY DO

I'm not going to ask you to feel guilty. Guilt is a bad fuel. Here are three things that actually help.

Learn the name. People protect what they can name. Say it: gaur. Rhymes with "power" in many English pronunciations, and sounds closer to "gaoor" in its original Hindi. Either way, say it out loud and tell one other person.

Support the boring work. Organizations running protected-area management, anti-poaching patrols, wildlife corridors, and community compensation schemes in India and Southeast Asia are the ones turning concern into forest. Pick one that publishes its results and give it something regular, even small.

Travel the right way. If you ever visit a reserve in India or Southeast Asia, choose operators who follow park rules, keep distance, and employ local guides. Tourism income is one of the strongest arguments a government has for keeping a forest standing.

That's it. No grand gesture.

Just attention, then money, then presence.

In that order.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THREE MYTHS THAT NEED TO DIE

Myth one: "It's just a big cow." No. A domestic cow was shaped by a few thousand years of human selection for milk and meat. The gaur was shaped by millions of years of forest, heat, predators, and hunger. Different pressures, different machine.

Myth two: "Animals that big are safe." The opposite is true. Large body size is one of the strongest predictors of extinction risk in mammals. Big bodies mean slow breeding, large territories, and constant friction with people.

Myth three: "Wildlife conservation is a distant, abstract problem." It's a forest. It's a herd. It's a calf that either survives its first year or doesn't. It happens in real places, to real animals, on a timeline measured in your lifetime.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

A YEAR IN THE LIFE OF A GIANT

The dry season is when the story changes.

Through the cooler, drier months, which in much of India run roughly from winter into early summer, the loners come back. Adult bulls leave their solitary routines and search out the herds, moving from group to group, checking, comparing, competing.

Bulls at this time are described as vocal and restless. Deep calls carry across the hills. Contests between rivals are mostly about posture, size, and display, with outright fights less common than the horns suggest.
Then the monsoon arrives.

Water everywhere. Grass exploding. Calves hitting the ground into a world of green.
By the time the dry heat returns, those calves are strong enough to follow the herd.

It's an annual cycle that has repeated, without a single missed turn, for longer than human farming has existed.
And it only continues if the forest it runs on is still standing.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

TEN FAST FACTS TO STEAL

Screenshot these. Use them at dinner.

The gaur is the largest wild bovine on Earth.

Big bulls can weigh close to a tonne and stand around 2 meters tall at the shoulder.

It is wild cattle, not a bison.

The back ridge is built on elongated vertebral spines that anchor the muscle holding up the head and horns.

Adult bulls have few natural enemies. Tigers mostly target calves and weaker animals.

A cow gives birth to a single calf after roughly nine months of pregnancy.

Herds are often around eight to a dozen animals, led by an experienced older female.

The species is listed as Vulnerable, with a world population counted in the tens of thousands at most.

The first cloned endangered animal ever born was a gaur named Noah, in 2001.

It is gone from Sri Lanka, and shrinking across much of the rest of its range.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

WHAT THIS REALLY IS ABOUT

Strip away the biology and the numbers and there's a simpler idea underneath.

Power and fragility are not opposites.

The gaur is one of the most physically powerful animals in its world. It is also one of the most exposed. Both statements are true at the same time.

We tend to think that strong things survive.

History keeps saying otherwise.

What survives is what we decide to leave room for.

A tonne of muscle can walk out of a forest and into a headline for the last time. And the only thing between that outcome and a different one is whether enough people care before the numbers get too small to argue with.

Every species that ever disappeared had a last ordinary day. A day when it was still out there, still eating, still moving through its home, and nobody marked the date because nobody knew it was close.

We don't have to repeat that.

We still have the chance to be the generation that noticed in time.

Next time a giant crosses your screen, don't treat it as background. Treat it as a roll call. Every view is a small vote that this animal still matters, and votes like that are how forests get saved.

So here's my ask.

Don't just watch the video above once.

Watch it the way you'd watch something you were never promised you'd get to see again.

Because with animals like this one, nobody is promising.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

How?

Hold that question. We'll come back to it.

Camouflage, on an animal the size of a van.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

SIZE IS A PROBLEM. THE GAUR SOLVED IT.

Being big is hard.

It tends to be most active in the cooler hours: early morning and late afternoon into dusk. Midday is for shade and rest. It uses water and mud to dump heat. It lives in hilly, forested country where shade is never far away.

Nothing about this is accidental. Every habit is a patch on a physics problem.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE FUEL BILL

An adult gaur needs to eat a staggering amount.

Cattle-sized herbivores typically need a few percent of their body weight in dry food every day. For a gaur, that points to something on the order of 20 kilograms or more of dry matter, which is far more in fresh grass and leaves.

That is not a snack. That is a full-time job.

It grazes on grasses. It browses leaves, shoots, and bamboo. It eats fruit when it can. It strips bark. And it seeks out natural mineral licks, spots in the earth where salts and minerals are exposed, because a plant diet alone does not always supply everything a body this big needs.

Notice what that really means.

Every day, a gaur has to find enough food to power a small car's worth of muscle, in a forest that is shrinking, shared with people, farms, roads and livestock.

Now you understand why habitat is not a "nice to have" for this species.

Habitat is the entire engine.

WHY A TIGER THINKS TWICE
