THE NUMBER THAT SHOULD BOTHER YOU

The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists the gaur as Vulnerable.

The most-cited estimates for mature individuals fall somewhere in the range of roughly 13,000 to 30,000 animals across the whole of its range. And that range is not one clean block of forest. It is a scatter of patches, spread across India, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia.

The species is considered to have declined substantially across much of its range over the last few decades. It has already been lost from some places where it once lived, including Sri Lanka.

Let that sink in.

Total world population, by the optimistic count: less than a third of a single football stadium crowd.

Spread across nine countries.

Broken into islands.

And that's for an animal that can weigh nearly a tonne and fear almost nothing in its forest.

It tells you something uncomfortable.

Size does not protect you from us.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

WHAT ACTUALLY KILLS A GIANT

Not predators. Not the dry season. Not old age.

Three things, mostly.

One: habitat loss. Forests cut, converted to farms, roads, plantations, and reservoirs. A gaur's home range has to contain food, water, shade, and mineral licks. Chop the range into islands and the herd has nowhere to go.

Two: hunting. In many parts of its range, gaur are hunted for meat, and in some places for trophies or traditional uses. Even low levels of hunting, on a slow-breeding species, add up faster than people expect.

Three: disease. Gaur are cattle. They catch cattle diseases. In the past, epidemics such as rinderpest, spread from domestic livestock, wiped out huge numbers of wild cattle and related wildlife across Asia and Africa. Rinderpest was declared globally eradicated in 2011, one of only two diseases ever wiped out on purpose. But foot-and-mouth disease and other livestock illnesses remain a real threat when wild herds share grazing land with domestic cattle.

Look at that list.

Not one of them is a story of a stronger animal beating the gaur.

Every one of them is a story about what we built around it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE TIME WE TRIED TO CLONE ONE

In January 2001, a calf was born in Iowa.

Its mother was an ordinary domestic cow.

Its genetic parent was a gaur.

The calf was named Noah. He was the first cloned animal of an endangered species. Scientists had taken cells from a gaur, placed the genetic material into an egg from a domestic cow, and brought the pregnancy to term in a cow that was not even the same species.

It was a headline for about a week.

Noah lived for roughly two days. He died of a common infection, a dysentery-type illness that researchers said was not tied to the cloning itself.

Think about the symbolism for a second.

We can copy the genome of a giant. We can persuade a different species to carry it. We can do it with lab equipment that fits on a table.

And we still can't reliably keep wild herds alive in a forest.

That's not a failure of science.

That's a statement about priorities.

Technology is excellent at producing a single miracle. It is terrible at doing the boring, expensive, unglamorous work of protecting a place.

A cloned calf makes the news.

A protected corridor of forest doesn't. But it's the corridor that actually keeps a species alive.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE DOMESTIC COUSIN NOBODY TALKS ABOUT

Here's another twist.

In the hills of northeastern India and neighboring regions, there's a semi-domesticated bovine called the mithun, or gayal. It's a large, heavily built animal, and it's closely related to the gaur. Many researchers consider it either a domesticated form of the gaur or a gaur-cattle hybrid lineage. The exact origin is still debated.

Whichever it is, it points to an old and surprising relationship.

People have lived alongside this family of animals for a very long time. In some communities the mithun carries real cultural weight. It features in rituals, in status, in social life.

So the wild form is not an alien. It's a long-lost neighbor.

And that makes its decline stranger.

We took the tamed version into our homes and our traditions.

And we let the original slip out of the forest.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

WHY THE BIG ONES ARE THE HARDEST TO SAVE

There is a cruel pattern in conservation.

The bigger the animal, the more space it needs. The more space it needs, the more it collides with us. The more it collides with us, the less we tolerate it.

A gaur does not need much from humans. It just needs to be left alone, with enough forest to move through.

But a hungry herd near a village crop is a conflict. A gaur wandering onto a road is a hazard. A large animal that shows up in a plantation or on the edge of a town makes news, and rarely good news.

Think of what coexistence actually demands.

Land set aside that produces no immediate income. Corridors that connect one forest to another. Compensation for farmers who lose crops, so that anger doesn't turn into poison or a snare. Rangers who are paid and equipped. Local communities who benefit from the animals being alive.

None of that is glamorous.

All of it works.

The places where gaur populations are stable or recovering almost always have the same ingredients: strong protection, genuine enforcement, and people who gain more from a living forest than a cleared one.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WHAT A CAMERA TRAP KNOWS THAT YOU DON'T
Scientists track animals like this with remote cameras strapped to trees.
They trigger on heat and motion. They work day and night, in monsoon and drought. And they keep producing footage of animals that behave very differently when they believe nobody is watching.

A big herbivore in an unobserved forest is calm. Methodical. It has routes it has walked for years. It knows where the water is, and when.

That's the thing about wildlife footage that gets lost in the era of the fast scroll.

You are not seeing a performance.

You are seeing an animal going about its business in a system it has been tuned to for hundreds of thousands of years.

The slowness is the point.

The patience is the point.

The sheer calm of something that doesn't need to prove it is dangerous, because everything around it already knows.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE ONLY QUESTION THAT MATTERS

We live in an odd moment.

We can build machines that write essays, model proteins, and generate video of things that never existed.

We can put a camera in your pocket that sees better than any eye in nature.

And meanwhile, a creature that weighs nearly as much as a small car, that has survived for hundreds of thousands of years, that sits in the middle of an ecosystem holding it together, is quietly running out of forest.

Not because it's weak.

Because nobody was looking.

That's the entire problem, stated as plainly as it can be.

Extinction does not announce itself. It doesn't arrive with a siren. It arrives as a quiet drop in a number nobody was checking, in a forest nobody was visiting, in a species nobody could name.

Attention is the first form of protection.

Which is why a short clip of a gaur, moving through its habitat at its own pace, is not a throwaway piece of content.

It's evidence.

It's a record that this animal is still here, right now, in your lifetime, in your generation, doing what it has always done.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THREE THINGS YOU CAN ACTUALLY DO

I'm not going to ask you to feel guilty. Guilt is a bad fuel. Here are three things that actually help.

Learn the name. People protect what they can name. Say it: gaur. Rhymes with "power" in many English pronunciations, and sounds closer to "gaoor" in its original Hindi. Either way, say it out loud and tell one other person.

Support the boring work. Organizations running protected-area management, anti-poaching patrols, wildlife corridors, and community compensation schemes in India and Southeast Asia are the ones turning concern into forest. Pick one that publishes its results and give it something regular, even small.

Travel the right way. If you ever visit a reserve in India or Southeast Asia, choose operators who follow park rules, keep distance, and employ local guides. Tourism income is one of the strongest arguments a government has for keeping a forest standing.

That's it. No grand gesture.

Just attention, then money, then presence.

In that order.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THREE MYTHS THAT NEED TO DIE

Myth one: "It's just a big cow." No. A domestic cow was shaped by a few thousand years of human selection for milk and meat. The gaur was shaped by millions of years of forest, heat, predators, and hunger. Different pressures, different machine.

Myth two: "Animals that big are safe." The opposite is true. Large body size is one of the strongest predictors of extinction risk in mammals. Big bodies mean slow breeding, large territories, and constant friction with people.

Myth three: "Wildlife conservation is a distant, abstract problem." It's a forest. It's a herd. It's a calf that either survives its first year or doesn't. It happens in real places, to real animals, on a timeline measured in your lifetime.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

A YEAR IN THE LIFE OF A GIANT

The dry season is when the story changes.

Through the cooler, drier months, which in much of India run roughly from winter into early summer, the loners come back. Adult bulls leave their solitary routines and search out the herds, moving from group to group, checking, comparing, competing.

Bulls at this time are described as vocal and restless. Deep calls carry across the hills. Contests between rivals are mostly about posture, size, and display, with outright fights less common than the horns suggest.
Then the monsoon arrives.

Water everywhere. Grass exploding. Calves hitting the ground into a world of green.
By the time the dry heat returns, those calves are strong enough to follow the herd.

It's an annual cycle that has repeated, without a single missed turn, for longer than human farming has existed.
And it only continues if the forest it runs on is still standing.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

TEN FAST FACTS TO STEAL

Screenshot these. Use them at dinner.

The gaur is the largest wild bovine on Earth.

Big bulls can weigh close to a tonne and stand around 2 meters tall at the shoulder.

It is wild cattle, not a bison.

The back ridge is built on elongated vertebral spines that anchor the muscle holding up the head and horns.

Adult bulls have few natural enemies. Tigers mostly target calves and weaker animals.

A cow gives birth to a single calf after roughly nine months of pregnancy.

Herds are often around eight to a dozen animals, led by an experienced older female.

The species is listed as Vulnerable, with a world population counted in the tens of thousands at most.

The first cloned endangered animal ever born was a gaur named Noah, in 2001.

It is gone from Sri Lanka, and shrinking across much of the rest of its range.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

WHAT THIS REALLY IS ABOUT

Strip away the biology and the numbers and there's a simpler idea underneath.

Power and fragility are not opposites.

The gaur is one of the most physically powerful animals in its world. It is also one of the most exposed. Both statements are true at the same time.

We tend to think that strong things survive.

History keeps saying otherwise.

What survives is what we decide to leave room for.

A tonne of muscle can walk out of a forest and into a headline for the last time. And the only thing between that outcome and a different one is whether enough people care before the numbers get too small to argue with.

Every species that ever disappeared had a last ordinary day. A day when it was still out there, still eating, still moving through its home, and nobody marked the date because nobody knew it was close.

We don't have to repeat that.

We still have the chance to be the generation that noticed in time.

Next time a giant crosses your screen, don't treat it as background. Treat it as a roll call. Every view is a small vote that this animal still matters, and votes like that are how forests get saved.

So here's my ask.

Don't just watch the video above once.

Watch it the way you'd watch something you were never promised you'd get to see again.

Because with animals like this one, nobody is promising.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

If this changed how you see a creature you'd never heard of this morning, repost it. Someone in your feed has never heard the word gaur, and they're exactly one post away from caring.

Follow for more animals you didn't know you needed to know about.

Odessa, Texas / The Permian Basin 
A Journey Through the Decades
From Bonham Junior High to the Golden Years in the Permian Basin
Introduction
We were the last of the war babies and the first edge of the baby boom
generation. We grew up in Odessa, Texas, during a time when the
Permian Basin seemed destined to power America forever. We witnessed
the end of steam locomotives, the rise of television, the birth of the
Space Age, the Vietnam War, moon landings, oil booms and busts, and
eventually the arrival of computers and the Internet.
This is the story of one generation, the Permian High School Class of
1962, and of the city that shaped us.
________________________________
Chapter 1
Bonham Junior High: The Late 1950s
If you attended Bonham Junior High in the late 1950s, you might
remember voting on the name, mascot, and colors for the new Permian
High School. None of us realized at the time that the school would
someday become famous throughout Texas and beyond. It was simply the
new school on the north side, a place where we hoped to end up once we
survived junior high.
Bonham could be a rough place for a seventh grader. Hazing was
considered almost a rite of passage. Older boys might make a newcomer
push a penny across the floor with his nose or invent some other
embarrassment. Looking back, it sounds cruel, but that was simply how
things worked.
We quickly learned there were divisions in Odessa. People judged where
you lived, what your parents did for a living, and how much money they
made. The railroad tracks separated more than neighborhoods. South
Side was considered another world. Most north-side kids were warned
not to go wandering there after dark.
Inside Bonham there were different tribes. The athletes dominated the
sports fields. The thugs wore their jeans low, placed taps on their
shoes, smoked cigarettes, and seemed to challenge authority every
chance they got. Most of us floated somewhere between the two groups.
There was no air conditioning. West Texas heat poured through the
windows. Fistfights after school were common enough that they rarely
attracted much attention. News traveled through the grapevine long
before social media existed.
Most students walked home. A few rode bicycles, though by junior high
that no longer carried much status. Coolness came from other things.
If you owned a motorcycle at fourteen or fifteen, people noticed. I
rode an Allstate motorcycle during ninth grade and thought I was doing
pretty well.
The legendary Mr. Macintire led the Bonham band. He was probably one
of the finest band directors Odessa ever had and one of the craziest
men I ever encountered in education. I lasted exactly one day under
his instruction.
Even then, change was coming. Odessa was growing, Permian High School
was opening, and our generation was moving toward a decade none of us
could possibly imagine.
________________________________
Chapter 2
Ninth Grade and the End of Childhood
By ninth grade, everything seemed to be changing at once.
Our bodies were changing. Our interests were changing. Even the tools
we used in school were changing. Fountain pens were slowly being
replaced by ballpoint pens.
The world itself appeared to be speeding up.
Rock and roll had swept across America. Elvis Presley had been drafted
and sent to Germany. Fidel Castro had taken control of Cuba. Alaska
became the forty-ninth state, meaning Texas was no longer the nation's
largest state. Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens, and the Big Bopper died in
a plane crash that later became known as "The Day the Music Died."
Television fascinated us. Most programs were still black and white.
Families gathered together each evening to watch the same shows.
Stations often signed off at midnight. Before programming began, an
Indian-head test pattern filled the screen.
If your television broke, you could remove the vacuum tubes and carry
them to Cabel's to test them. If one had gone bad, replacements were
available right there at the store.
Many teenagers worked after school. Some sacked groceries at Bill
Sears or Piggly Wiggly. Others carried newspaper routes. The Odessa
American was still an afternoon newspaper.
School dances, the ninth-grade prom, football games, and telephone
conversations occupied our lives. Many afternoons were spent listening
to KECK radio, and many nights ended with KOMA drifting in through the
darkness.
By then most of us were already deciding who we wanted to become.
________________________________
Chapter 3
Entering Permian
Permian High School felt like a completely different world.
The social divisions we had known at Bonham became even more obvious.
There were athletes, scholars, band members, cheerleaders, and
troublemakers. Students were judged by clothes, hairstyles, cars,
grades, and athletic ability.
The football players wore their status proudly. The thugs favored
low-slung jeans and ducktail haircuts. The academic crowd usually
looked somewhere in between.
Girls faced strict dress codes. No pants. No jeans. Spaghetti straps
could get you sent home. Going steady meant loaning your football
jacket, band jacket, or choir jacket to a girl.
Pep rallies filled the auditorium. Football ruled everything.
Cheerleaders led chants while players promised victory.
Breaking rules could earn licks from a paddle or a trip to D-Hall.
Three-day suspensions were considered serious punishment. Counselors
would come later.
The school snack bar sold candy, pencils, paper, and soft drinks.
Students could leave campus for lunch. Fifty cents would buy a
hamburger, French fries, and a cherry Coke at Watts Burger or one of
the many drive-ins.
By then many students were experimenting with cigarettes, chewing
tobacco, and occasionally beer. A surprising number gathered before
school at the telephone company building across from Permian,
cigarettes in hand.
We thought we understood the world.
We did not.
________________________________
Chapter 4
Summer of 1960
The summer of 1960 belonged to teenagers.
Grant Street became Odessa's version of Main Street. Teenagers cruised
from one drive-in to another, visiting places like Tommie's, Days,
Speedway, Nick's, Danny's, Park Inn, and A&W.
The Speedway was famous for its colorful drinks and plastic stir
sticks topped with miniature animals. The Park Inn remained a favorite
gathering place.
Across town, South Side and Ector students had their own territory
around Murphy Street and the Frost Top.
Most evenings began with the simple phrase:
"I'm going to get a Coke."
Parents often knew that meant something much larger.
Cars cruised endlessly. Drag races occurred. Raw eggs occasionally
flew through open windows. Fistfights were arranged. Friendships
formed. Future husbands and wives met.
We were sixteen-year-old bodies carrying twelve-year-old wisdom.
Drive-in theaters were another summer ritual. Odessa had five of them.
Speakers hung from the car window. Double features were standard.
Cartoons played before the movies. The bouncing ball encouraged
sing-alongs.
A breakdown in the projection booth produced a symphony of impatient car horns.
For some teenagers, the drive-in theater had very little to do with the movie.
________________________________
Chapter 5
The Last of the War Babies
When the 1960-61 school year began, we entered our junior year at
Permian High School.
World War II had ended only fifteen years earlier. Looking back, our
class occupied a unique place. We were among the last students
directly shaped by a generation that had lived through the Depression
and fought the war.
Childhood was disappearing.
Bicycles, lunch boxes, marbles, coloring books, and cartoons faded into memory.
Christmas presents became practical.
Most of us worked after school. Gasoline averaged twenty-five cents a
gallon, and fierce price wars sometimes pushed it down to 17.9 cents.
Older friends bought beer. Paper driver's licenses occasionally
developed "improved" birth dates. Some drive-ins served draft beer
curbside.
The Park Inn became legendary.
Football remained the center of school life. Permian finished 8-3 that
season. The homecoming bonfire tradition began.
The band could be heard every morning before class. The members seemed
to belong to their own secret society.
P.E. class meant laps, touch football, soccer, basketball, and the
dreaded rope climb.
Principal Gail Smith guided the school. Teachers who remain vivid in
memory include Mr. Cariker, Mr. Crawley, Ms. Dial, Ms. Doyle, Mr.
Jacobs, and Mr. Tiner.
Breakfast was usually Cheerios or Post Toasties. By mid-morning our
stomachs often growled loudly enough that we were certain everyone
could hear.
________________________________
Chapter 6
Senior Year: 1961-62
By senior year we had reached the summit.
Twelve years of school were nearly over.
Cars became increasingly important. Hot rods, fuzzy dice, pinstriping,
glass packs, and four-on-the-floor transmissions dominated
conversations.
Songs like "Runaway," "Crying," "I Fall to Pieces," and "Take Good
Care of My Baby" filled radios.
Television favorites included Gunsmoke, Bonanza, Red Skelton, and Candid Camera.
Graduation seemed both exciting and frightening.
The senior prom arrived.
So did adulthood.
Some classmates became roughnecks, welders, mechanics, soldiers,
cashiers, teachers, housewives, or college students.
The class of 1962 stepped into a world that would soon be transformed
by war, politics, and technology.
________________________________
Chapter 7
Assassinations, Vietnam, and the Space Race
Three forces shaped our generation more than any others.
The first was political violence.
John F. Kennedy's assassination in Dallas in 1963 stunned the nation.
We watched Lee Harvey Oswald killed on live television two days later.
Lyndon Baines Johnson, another Texan, became president.
Martin Luther King Jr. and Robert Kennedy were both assassinated in 1968.
The second force was Vietnam.
By late 1967 nearly half a million Americans served there. Ultimately
more than 2.7 million Americans would serve in Vietnam and over 58,000
would die.
Some of our classmates went.
Some returned changed forever.
Some never returned at all.
The third force was the Space Race.
We were the "Duck and Cover" generation. We believed beating the
Russians mattered.
Odessa's dark skies sometimes revealed satellites crossing overhead.
The Apollo program pushed forward despite setbacks, including the
tragic fire that killed Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee.
The moon seemed impossibly far away.
Yet somehow it no longer felt unreachable.
________________________________
Chapter 8
The 1970s
The 1970s found most of us firmly planted in adulthood.
We were husbands and wives. Parents. Workers. Veterans. College
graduates. Oil-field hands.
Many were still trying to figure life out.
Disco arrived, and Odessa danced right along with the rest of the country.
The local nightlife revolved around Herb Gram's clubs. The Shadows
played pop music. Across Andrews Highway, the Stardust catered to
country fans.
For a brief and ridiculous moment, streaking became a national craze.
The Gatlin Brothers became Odessa's hometown stars.
In 1972, Permian High School won the state championship and was named
national co-champion. Mojo became more than a nickname. It became a
rallying cry.
Nationally, Nixon resigned. The Vietnam War ended. The oil embargo
created recession. Elvis died. Margaret Thatcher rose to power in
Britain. The Iran hostage crisis began.
Locally, the Permian Basin suffered through painful boom-and-bust
cycles. Businesses closed. Buildings stood empty. Workers departed in
search of opportunity elsewhere.
Yet Odessa endured.
It always had.
________________________________
Chapter 9
The 1980s
The babies of the forties and fifties entered middle age.
Most of us passed forty.
Some called the 1980s the "Decade of Decadence."
Ronald Reagan occupied the White House for nearly the entire decade.
Many of us now had teenagers of our own.
Permian football reached legendary status. State championships came in
1980, 1984, and 1989. The 1989 team added a national championship.
Mojo was everywhere.
The world brought dramatic change.
CNN arrived.
Personal computers entered ordinary homes.
The Challenger exploded.
The AIDS epidemic spread.
Chernobyl shocked the world.
The Berlin Wall fell.
MTV revolutionized music.
Meanwhile we watched Dallas, Cheers, CHiPs, and Hill Street Blues
while listening to Olivia Newton-John, Pink Floyd, George Jones, Dolly
Parton, Conway Twitty, and a young Garth Brooks.
Many of us noticed new gray hairs.
Some noticed a few extra pounds.
By the end of the decade, many had become grandparents.
Life was moving faster than ever.
________________________________
Chapter 10
Approaching Fifty: The 1990s
By the middle of the 1990s, most of us were approaching fifty years old.
Half a century.
The phrase "golden years" began appearing in conversation, half joke
and half hope.
Operation Desert Storm introduced another generation to war.
Bill Clinton was elected president.
The Dallas Cowboys became America's Team once again.
The Internet arrived.
eBay appeared.
The iMac was introduced.
Scientists cloned Dolly the sheep.
Country music flourished with Garth Brooks, George Strait, and Brooks
& Dunn. Television gave us The West Wing and The Sopranos. Movies
included Titanic, Casino, and The Shawshank Redemption.
The decade also produced tragedies, controversies, and unforgettable
headlines. Oklahoma City. Waco. O.J. Simpson. Ruby Ridge.
The world we had entered as children scarcely resembled the one around us now.
________________________________
Epilogue
Looking Back
When we walked the halls of Permian High School in 1960, none of us
could have imagined everything we would witness.
We saw the end of segregation and the beginning of space exploration.
We watched Kennedy's funeral, Armstrong's moonwalk, the fall of the
Berlin Wall, and the birth of the Internet.
We survived recessions, oil busts, wars, social upheaval, and personal
heartbreaks.
Some classmates became wealthy. Some struggled. Some were taken far
too early. Others remain with us today.
What binds us together is not simply that we attended the same school.
It is that we traveled through one of the most extraordinary periods
in American history together.
We were the last of the war babies.
We were the Class of 1962. Hollywood even made a movie about us. "American Graffiti"
And for a little while, under the vast West Texas sky, the Permian
Basin was the center of our world

The world itself appeared to be speeding up.
Rock and roll had swept across America. Elvis Presley had been drafted
and sent to Germany. Fidel Castro had taken control of Cuba. Alaska
became the forty-ninth state, meaning Texas was no longer the nation's
largest state. Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens, and the Big Bopper died in
a plane crash that later became known as "The Day the Music Died."
Television fascinated us. Most programs were still black and white.
Families gathered together each evening to watch the same shows.
Stations often signed off at midnight. Before programming began, an
Indian-head test pattern filled the screen.
If your television broke, you could remove the vacuum tubes and carry
them to Cabel's to test them. If one had gone bad, replacements were
available right there at the store.
Many teenagers worked after school. Some sacked groceries at Bill
Sears or Piggly Wiggly. Others carried newspaper routes. The Odessa
American was still an afternoon newspaper.
School dances, the ninth-grade prom, football games, and telephone
conversations occupied our lives. Many afternoons were spent listening
to KECK radio, and many nights ended with KOMA drifting in through the
darkness.
By then most of us were already deciding who we wanted to become.
________________________________
Chapter 3
Entering Permian
Permian High School felt like a completely different world.
The social divisions we had known at Bonham became even more obvious.
There were athletes, scholars, band members, cheerleaders, and
troublemakers. Students were judged by clothes, hairstyles, cars,
grades, and athletic ability.
The football players wore their status proudly. The thugs favored
low-slung jeans and ducktail haircuts. The academic crowd usually
looked somewhere in between.
Girls faced strict dress codes. No pants. No jeans. Spaghetti straps
could get you sent home. Going steady meant loaning your football
jacket, band jacket, or choir jacket to a girl.
Pep rallies filled the auditorium. Football ruled everything.
Cheerleaders led chants while players promised victory.
Breaking rules could earn licks from a paddle or a trip to D-Hall.
Three-day suspensions were considered serious punishment. Counselors
would come later.
The school snack bar sold candy, pencils, paper, and soft drinks.
Students could leave campus for lunch. Fifty cents would buy a
hamburger, French fries, and a cherry Coke at Watts Burger or one of
the many drive-ins.
By then many students were experimenting with cigarettes, chewing
tobacco, and occasionally beer. A surprising number gathered before
school at the telephone company building across from Permian,
cigarettes in hand.
We thought we understood the world.
We did not.
________________________________
Chapter 4
Summer of 1960
The summer of 1960 belonged to teenagers.
Grant Street became Odessa's version of Main Street. Teenagers cruised
from one drive-in to another, visiting places like Tommie's, Days,
Speedway, Nick's, Danny's, Park Inn, and A&W.
The Speedway was famous for its colorful drinks and plastic stir
sticks topped with miniature animals. The Park Inn remained a favorite
gathering place.
Across town, South Side and Ector students had their own territory
around Murphy Street and the Frost Top.
Most evenings began with the simple phrase:
"I'm going to get a Coke."
Parents often knew that meant something much larger.
Cars cruised endlessly. Drag races occurred. Raw eggs occasionally
flew through open windows. Fistfights were arranged. Friendships
formed. Future husbands and wives met.
We were sixteen-year-old bodies carrying twelve-year-old wisdom.
Drive-in theaters were another summer ritual. Odessa had five of them.
Speakers hung from the car window. Double features were standard.
Cartoons played before the movies. The bouncing ball encouraged
sing-alongs.
A breakdown in the projection booth produced a symphony of impatient car horns.
For some teenagers, the drive-in theater had very little to do with the movie.
________________________________
Chapter 5
The Last of the War Babies
When the 1960-61 school year began, we entered our junior year at
Permian High School.
World War II had ended only fifteen years earlier. Looking back, our
class occupied a unique place. We were among the last students
directly shaped by a generation that had lived through the Depression
and fought the war.
Childhood was disappearing.
Bicycles, lunch boxes, marbles, coloring books, and cartoons faded into memory.
Christmas presents became practical.
Most of us worked after school. Gasoline averaged twenty-five cents a
gallon, and fierce price wars sometimes pushed it down to 17.9 cents.
Older friends bought beer. Paper driver's licenses occasionally
developed "improved" birth dates. Some drive-ins served draft beer
curbside.
The Park Inn became legendary.
Football remained the center of school life. Permian finished 8-3 that
season. The homecoming bonfire tradition began.
The band could be heard every morning before class. The members seemed
to belong to their own secret society.
P.E. class meant laps, touch football, soccer, basketball, and the
dreaded rope climb.
Principal Gail Smith guided the school. Teachers who remain vivid in
memory include Mr. Cariker, Mr. Crawley, Ms. Dial, Ms. Doyle, Mr.
Jacobs, and Mr. Tiner.
Breakfast was usually Cheerios or Post Toasties. By mid-morning our
stomachs often growled loudly enough that we were certain everyone
could hear.
________________________________
Chapter 6
Senior Year: 1961-62
By senior year we had reached the summit.
Twelve years of school were nearly over.
Cars became increasingly important. Hot rods, fuzzy dice, pinstriping,
glass packs, and four-on-the-floor transmissions dominated
conversations.
Songs like "Runaway," "Crying," "I Fall to Pieces," and "Take Good
Care of My Baby" filled radios.
Television favorites included Gunsmoke, Bonanza, Red Skelton, and Candid Camera.
Graduation seemed both exciting and frightening.
The senior prom arrived.
So did adulthood.
Some classmates became roughnecks, welders, mechanics, soldiers,
cashiers, teachers, housewives, or college students.
The class of 1962 stepped into a world that would soon be transformed
by war, politics, and technology.
________________________________
Chapter 7
Assassinations, Vietnam, and the Space Race
Three forces shaped our generation more than any others.
The first was political violence.
John F. Kennedy's assassination in Dallas in 1963 stunned the nation.
We watched Lee Harvey Oswald killed on live television two days later.
Lyndon Baines Johnson, another Texan, became president.
Martin Luther King Jr. and Robert Kennedy were both assassinated in 1968.
The second force was Vietnam.
By late 1967 nearly half a million Americans served there. Ultimately
more than 2.7 million Americans would serve in Vietnam and over 58,000
would die.
Some of our classmates went.
Some returned changed forever.
Some never returned at all.
The third force was the Space Race.
We were the "Duck and Cover" generation. We believed beating the
Russians mattered.
Odessa's dark skies sometimes revealed satellites crossing overhead.
The Apollo program pushed forward despite setbacks, including the
tragic fire that killed Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee.
The moon seemed impossibly far away.
Yet somehow it no longer felt unreachable.
________________________________
Chapter 8
The 1970s
The 1970s found most of us firmly planted in adulthood.
We were husbands and wives. Parents. Workers. Veterans. College
graduates. Oil-field hands.
Many were still trying to figure life out.
Disco arrived, and Odessa danced right along with the rest of the country.
The local nightlife revolved around Herb Gram's clubs. The Shadows
played pop music. Across Andrews Highway, the Stardust catered to
country fans.
For a brief and ridiculous moment, streaking became a national craze.
The Gatlin Brothers became Odessa's hometown stars.
In 1972, Permian High School won the state championship and was named
national co-champion. Mojo became more than a nickname. It became a
rallying cry.
Nationally, Nixon resigned. The Vietnam War ended. The oil embargo
created recession. Elvis died. Margaret Thatcher rose to power in
Britain. The Iran hostage crisis began.
Locally, the Permian Basin suffered through painful boom-and-bust
cycles. Businesses closed. Buildings stood empty. Workers departed in
search of opportunity elsewhere.
Yet Odessa endured.
It always had.
________________________________
Chapter 9
The 1980s
The babies of the forties and fifties entered middle age.
Most of us passed forty.
Some called the 1980s the "Decade of Decadence."
Ronald Reagan occupied the White House for nearly the entire decade.
Many of us now had teenagers of our own.
Permian football reached legendary status. State championships came in
1980, 1984, and 1989. The 1989 team added a national championship.
Mojo was everywhere.
The world brought dramatic change.
CNN arrived.
Personal computers entered ordinary homes.
The Challenger exploded.
The AIDS epidemic spread.
Chernobyl shocked the world.
The Berlin Wall fell.
MTV revolutionized music.
Meanwhile we watched Dallas, Cheers, CHiPs, and Hill Street Blues
while listening to Olivia Newton-John, Pink Floyd, George Jones, Dolly
Parton, Conway Twitty, and a young Garth Brooks.
Many of us noticed new gray hairs.
Some noticed a few extra pounds.
By the end of the decade, many had become grandparents.
Life was moving faster than ever.
________________________________
Chapter 10
Approaching Fifty: The 1990s
By the middle of the 1990s, most of us were approaching fifty years old.
Half a century.
The phrase "golden years" began appearing in conversation, half joke
and half hope.
Operation Desert Storm introduced another generation to war.
Bill Clinton was elected president.
The Dallas Cowboys became America's Team once again.
The Internet arrived.
eBay appeared.
The iMac was introduced.
Scientists cloned Dolly the sheep.
Country music flourished with Garth Brooks, George Strait, and Brooks
& Dunn. Television gave us The West Wing and The Sopranos. Movies
included Titanic, Casino, and The Shawshank Redemption.
The decade also produced tragedies, controversies, and unforgettable
headlines. Oklahoma City. Waco. O.J. Simpson. Ruby Ridge.
The world we had entered as children scarcely resembled the one around us now.
________________________________
Epilogue
Looking Back
When we walked the halls of Permian High School in 1960, none of us
could have imagined everything we would witness.
We saw the end of segregation and the beginning of space exploration.
We watched Kennedy's funeral, Armstrong's moonwalk, the fall of the
Berlin Wall, and the birth of the Internet.
We survived recessions, oil busts, wars, social upheaval, and personal
heartbreaks.
Some classmates became wealthy. Some struggled. Some were taken far
too early. Others remain with us today.
What binds us together is not simply that we attended the same school.
It is that we traveled through one of the most extraordinary periods
in American history together.
We were the last of the war babies.
We were the Class of 1962. Hollywood even made a movie about us. "American Graffiti"
And for a little while, under the vast West Texas sky, the Permian
Basin was the center of our world

text:
For years, when clients talked about river cruising, the conversation usually meant Europe.

- The Rhine.
- The Danube.
- Maybe the Douro.

That is changing quickly.

What has my attention now is where river cruising is expanding next.

India’s Brahmaputra.

Colombia’s Magdalena.

The Mekong through Vietnam and Cambodia.

The Nile continuing to grow.

And even more development on U.S. rivers.

Major brands are investing too. Viking is expanding into India. Scenic is following. AmaWaterways is building out Colombia and the Nile. New ships are coming to the Mekong.

As a travel advisor, I think this makes river cruising much more interesting.

These are no longer just scenic sailings between European cities.

They are becoming a way to explore places that can otherwise require a lot of complicated overland planning, while still unpacking once and keeping a consistent level of service.

That is a pretty compelling combination for travelers who want something immersive without giving up comfort.

I think the next wave of river cruising is going to be less about Europe.

And much more about access.

text:
Do you think the Vietnamese people are being criticized because of their race? I think it’s worth considering that Japanese people can also face criticism for dancing in large groups in crowded public places without permission.

For example, a group of Japanese high school girls once danced together at Tokyo Disneyland, and it received a lot of criticism in Japan. The incident was even covered on morning news programs.

Videos of street dancing do circulate from time to time, but when the dancing obstructs other people, it can attract criticism. In other cases, the videos may simply not receive much attention.

So I think the criticism may be more about the location and the impact on other people than the nationality of those involved.

Do you think the Vietnamese people are being criticized because of their race? I think it’s worth considering that Japanese people can also face criticism for dancing in large groups in crowded public places without permission.

For example, a group of Japanese high school girls once danced together at Tokyo Disneyland, and it received a lot of criticism in Japan. The incident was even covered on morning news programs.

Videos of street dancing do circulate from time to time, but when the dancing obstructs other people, it can attract criticism. In other cases, the videos may simply not receive much attention.

So I think the criticism may be more about the location and the impact on other people than the nationality of those involved.

text:
A family that built a home with its life savings now lives in a shack on a relative’s land, still waiting for compensation. 

Residents march silently at night in matching shirts, hoping to save neighborhoods their families have lived in for generations. 

Across Việt Nam, from Hà Nội’s Vĩnh Hưng and the banks of the Red River to the new airport at Gia Bình, the state is taking land faster than it can rehouse the people who live on it. 

New rules now let officials seize homes before resettlement is ready. Compensation lags far behind market value, and thousands of resettlement apartments sit empty. 

Officials promise one thing and sign the opposite days later. Party leaders pledge “all my devotion” to the people, yet it is ordinary families who are asked to give everything. 

When the government then floated a proposal to let children donate organs, the public reaction was instant, and it showed how little trust is left.

Read more: https://t.co/46sfUehAZ7

text:
The Vietnam Phu Quoc tragedy brings into focus a little-known fact in India's tourism sector. 

Probably the biggest component of outbound international tourism from India is the "dealer incentive package." 

Here is how it works. Most brands have dealers. Think mobile phones, cement, servers, bathroom fittings, switch boards etc. How do marketers increase their sales? There are two types of strategies:

1. The "pull" strategy. You design a superior product. You build a killer brand that everyone wants. You price competitively. You make it available easily. You advertise aggressively. These are things that most people recognize immediately as "marketing." You "pull" the customer directly into buying.

Sadly, the pull strategy is not always feasible. Standing out in a commoditized space is not easy. Plus, there may be very strong incumbents whose brand recall you cannot easily match. So you supplement your "pull" strategy with something more insidious - the "push" strategy.

2. The "push" strategy. Say your bathroom tap is leaking. You need to buy a new tap. You immediately think of "Alpha" - you have seen its ads during IPL, its hoardings, etc. You go to the hardware store. He has "Alpha" but tells you to try a new, lesser known "Beta" instead. He sings its virtues and says how it is better than Alpha. Why is he doing it? Because Beta has employed a "push" strategy. They give the dealer a higher margin, better commissions, etc. So he is incentivized to "push" Beta on to you. You do not know if he genuinely loves Beta or is just getting paid to promote it to you.

Sometimes, there are grey areas. Drug companies for example are known to offer push incentives to doctors to prescribe their drugs. The now-defunct Byjus was notorious for offering push incentives to school teachers who got commissions if their students subscribed to it.

Push incentives for things like mobile phones, computers, cement, etc. are not so ethically gray. And a common incentive is of the type, "Sell 1000 units of my product and Thailand Trip free. Sell 2000 and Japan trip free. Sell 3000 and Paris Trip free." This causes retailers, who have otherwise very mundane lives, and often work in crowded, congested market areas, and dirty tier 2 and 3 towns, to put in more effort, to earn that additional freebee - the annual foreign trip.

Naturally these "incentive" trips cost money and eat into the brand's margins. One option is to raise prices, but that is a negative "pull" incentive that will decrease demand. Then the obvious thing to do is to cut costs on the incentive itself, while still delivering that tour package you promised. Offer a Vietnam trip with a boat ride to Phu Quoc, but at the bare minimum price. 

You sub-contract to a large outbound travel agency which bulk books hotels, air tickets, and airport transfer in India. But to handle the logistics in a foreign country like Vietnam, they further sub-contract to an inbound travel agency in Vietnam. Who further sub-contracts buses from one operator, boats from another, food from a third, etc. Margins are ultra-thin at the implementation end, with everyone saving money.

Sadly, many of these operators then skimp on essential features. Five extra people in a boat. Ignore if a few life jackets don't have belts. Bare-basics Indian food, because Indian food is expensive in these countries, but the tourists will not eat local cuisine. Plus you often have "that" kind of Indian tourist who is excited about "boys trip to Bangkok" and "hum ab daaru peeyenge."

I learnt a little bit about all of this many years ago from a tour guide who at that point spent 20+ days every month escorting these groups. I suspect one or a mix of all these factors may have led to the tragedy at Phu Quoc. Only a thorough, and hopefully unbiased enquiry will reveal how this tragedy came to be.

text:
#WATCH | ✈️🌍 Where did India travel in 2025? Short answer: Everywhere.

Vietnam emerged as the breakout star with a 133% jump in traffic, while OG favourites—Phuket, Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur—still ruled wishlists.
Closer home, Varanasi & Andamans saw ~20% growth, with UP the most visited state.

But the real shift? Indians travelled wider & deeper—from Ziro, Pasighat, Jagdalpur to solo escapes led by Delhi & Bengaluru.
New Year plans went global & personal—from yacht parties in the Philippines to Arctic saunas in Finland.

Driven by Gen Z (travel up 650%), India didn’t just travel more in 2025—
👉 It travelled further, younger & more personal. 🌏✨

#Varanasi #Indian #Delhi #NewYear @maryamf_writes

text:
What is the world’s most dynamic society in 2026? 
It’s Vietnam 🇻🇳!

We are just back from a wonderful family holiday in Vietnam. It is a most amazing place with extraordinary natural beauty, the most friendly people, exciting food, full of life.

Vietnam showed the world that a small developing nation could beat French colonialists and American imperialists. We visited many of the most remarkable sites of the horrible war - the citadel of Hue, Khe Sanh, Ap Bac and Saigon center where the last Americans fled in 1975.

But more striking than anything else is the dynamism of modern Vietnam. No nation today move forward with the same speed. People work hard and smart. The governing system is effective. Vietnam doesnt waste time making enemies. It’s a good friend of the US and China and everyone else.        
                                                  
* Vietnam has achieved a historic drop in poverty, reducing extreme rates from nearly 60% in the early 1990s down to 2-3% today.

* Vietnams economy expanded by 8.2% year-on-year in the first half of 2026, with the government targeting 11.9% growth in the second half to hit a double-digit full-year expansion.

*. Industrial production and manufacturing surged over 10.2% this year, powered heavily by high-tech processing, electronics - working with both China and the US.

* Vietnam is probably the worlds most succesful agricultural nation over the last decades. It was the world’s largest rice importer in the 1980s. It’s now one of the largest rice exporters. Vietnam is the second largest coffee exporter in the wolrd, next to Brazil only. No rocket science - only good policies.

* Vietnam is a miracle of education - it outperforms all nations in the world in tests of 15 years old in school - only exception is East Asian nations like Korea, Singapore and China.

Anyone interested in rapid development - please make a pilgrimage to Vietnam!

text:
Yesterday marked the 57th anniversary of the start of the Battle of Huế that began on January 31, 1968, during the Tet Offensive in the Vietnam War.

The battle lasted until March 2, 1968, making it one of the longest and bloodiest urban battles of the Vietnam War. North Vietnamese Army (NVA) and Viet Cong forces launched a surprise attack, seizing most of the city, including the historic Huế Citadel. U.S. Marines, South Vietnamese forces (ARVN), and U.S. Army units fought house-to-house to retake the city in intense combat.

Read the @WarInstitute case study @JaysonGeroux and I wrote detailing the battle and its lessons. Photo credit @JaysonGeroux https://t.co/AOUqhpXg1J

text:
Illuminating Hue’s Nhu Y River - a mesmerizing 'Lantern' ceremony, symbolises 'Hope and Peace' in Vietnam :

In the tranquil waters of the Nhu Y River in Hue, Vietnam, a captivating scene unfolds as women, dressed in traditional Vietnamese attire, engage in a ritual of hope and peace. With their iconic conical hats and graceful dresses, these women partake in an age-old tradition, setting about 4,000 flower lanterns adrift on the river. This enchanting ceremony, captured by photographer Nguyen Minh Tuan, is more than just a visual spectacle; it is a deeply symbolic act resonating with cultural significance and communal aspirations.

The lantern ceremony, a poignant and reflective tradition, represents the collective wishes of the local community. Each lantern, delicately placed on the water, carries prayers for health and good fortune. The act of releasing these lanterns is symbolic of letting go of past troubles and embracing a future filled with luck and tranquility. It is also a moment to remember and wish peace for departed relatives, connecting the present with the ancestral past.

As the lanterns, crafted from flowers and candles, gently float down the Nhu Y River, they create a mesmerizing display of light and color. The flickering candles reflect on the water, creating a peaceful and dreamlike atmosphere. This spectacle is not only a feast for the eyes but also a soul-soothing experience, embodying the essence of Vietnamese spiritual life.

The ceremony holds a special place in the cultural fabric of Hue, a city known for its rich history and cultural heritage. Hue, once the imperial capital of Vietnam, is no stranger to traditional rituals and ceremonies. This lantern ceremony is a testament to the city’s enduring cultural traditions and its deep connection with the natural and spiritual worlds.

For locals and visitors alike, the ceremony is an opportunity to partake in a shared cultural experience. It is a moment of collective reflection, an opportunity to pause and appreciate the beauty of simplicity and the power of community. The ritual is a reminder of the enduring human desire for peace, health, and happiness.

The lantern ceremony on the Nhu Y River is more than just a cultural event; it’s a spiritual journey and a celebration of life’s intangible values. It stands as a symbol of the Vietnamese people’s resilience, their reverence for nature, and their deep-seated belief in the power of goodwill and positive intentions. For those who witness it, ceremony is an unforgettable experience, offering a unique insight into the soul of Vietnamese culture and the timeless traditions that continue to shape the heart and spirit of Hue.

text:
DAY 1: Imperial City

Start early at the Imperial City. And when I say early, I mean around 7:30.  Hue gets HOT. There is plenty of shade inside the complex, but also plenty of walking between that shade.

🎟️ Entry: 200,000 VND

Give it at least 2.5–3 hours. Highly recommend visiting with a guide, or renting an audio guide for 100,000 VND.

This was the political and administrative centre of the Nguyen dynasty, with palaces, temples, courtyards and the Forbidden Purple City sitting inside a huge walled complex.

There is also a LOT to look at. Some areas were badly damaged, so you’ll move between restored buildings, ruins and reconstruction. 2/11

text:
Vietnam is famous for its vibrant and diverse street food culture. The streets of cities like Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City are lined with food stalls and open-air markets where you can find a wide variety of delicious and affordable meals.
Some popular street foods in Vietnam include pho, a traditional noodle soup made with broth, rice noodles, herbs, and meat (usually chicken or beef); bánh mì, a sandwich made with a baguette filled with various ingredients like grilled pork, pâté, pickled vegetables, and herbs; and bún chả, a dish made with grilled pork served with rice vermicelli noodles, herbs, and a dipping sauce.
Other popular street foods include spring rolls, grilled seafood, bánh xèo (savory pancakes), and various noodle dishes like bún bò Huế (spicy beef noodle soup) and mì Quảng (turmeric noodles with pork or shrimp).
One of the best things about Vietnamese street food is the variety and availability of vegetarian and vegan options. You can easily find dishes made with tofu, tempeh, vegetables, and fresh herbs at street food stalls and markets.
Overall, Vietnamese street food is a delicious, affordable, and essential part of experiencing the country’s rich culinary heritage.
The only thing,they don’t add pepper to their food! 😁😁😁 I actually tried their street food today. 🇻🇳🇻🇳🇻🇳🇻🇳

Some popular street foods in Vietnam include pho, a traditional noodle soup made with broth, rice noodles, herbs, and meat (usually chicken or beef); bánh mì, a sandwich made with a baguette filled with various ingredients like grilled pork, pâté, pickled vegetables, and herbs; and bún chả, a dish made with grilled pork served with rice vermicelli noodles, herbs, and a dipping sauce.
Other popular street foods include spring rolls, grilled seafood, bánh xèo (savory pancakes), and various noodle dishes like bún bò Huế (spicy beef noodle soup) and mì Quảng (turmeric noodles with pork or shrimp).
One of the best things about Vietnamese street food is the variety and availability of vegetarian and vegan options. You can easily find dishes made with tofu, tempeh, vegetables, and fresh herbs at street food stalls and markets.
Overall, Vietnamese street food is a delicious, affordable, and essential part of experiencing the country’s rich culinary heritage.

text:
🌏✨ Discover the Timeless Charm of Hue – Vietnam's Imperial Capital ✨🌏
🕌 Hue, the ancient capital of Vietnam, is a mesmerizing blend of history, culture, and natural beauty waiting to be explored! 🌿 From grand imperial palaces to serene rivers and enchanting pagodas, Hue offers an unforgettable journey back in time.
🌟 Why Hue Should Be on Your Travel List?
🏯 The Imperial City: Step into the UNESCO World Heritage Site where emperors once ruled. Marvel at its magnificent gates, intricate architecture, and vibrant history.
🌉 Perfume River: Take a boat ride on this iconic river, where legends meet breathtaking sunsets. 🌅
🕊️ Pagodas and Temples: Visit the Thien Mu Pagoda, standing gracefully by the river, and feel the serenity of centuries-old spiritual traditions.
🍲 Culinary Paradise: Hue’s cuisine is a feast for the senses! Try the royal-inspired dishes like Bun Bo Hue (spicy beef noodle soup) and banh khoai (crispy pancakes). 😋
🎨 Craft Villages: Discover traditional craftsmanship in nearby villages, from conical hats to fine embroidery.
🎶 A Symphony of Culture
Hue is not just a place; it’s an experience. Immerse yourself in the melodious sounds of ca Hue (traditional chamber music) performed on a dragon boat, surrounded by the glow of lanterns under the starry sky. 🌌🎵
📸 Instagram-Worthy Views
Hue is a photographer’s dream! Capture moments at the stunning Tomb of Emperor Khai Dinh, explore hidden corners of the Imperial City, or simply enjoy the lush green landscapes that stretch endlessly. 📷🌿
💬 Your Next Adventure Awaits!
Have you ever visited a city where history whispers in every corner? Share your favorite moments in Hue or ask us anything about this enchanting destination! 🌍👇
🛫 Plan your trip today and let Hue’s timeless beauty inspire your soul. 🌺

text:
Century Riverside Hotel Hue, Vietnam — Mini Review 😎

Staying here feels like living inside a postcard of Hue, Vietnam.
Right by the Perfume River, walkable to food, cafes, night walking street — aka wallet-friendly travel mode activated 💸😂

Rooms:
- Spacious, clean, bright. Open the curtains: river + breeze combo = instant poetry.
- Beds so comfy I almost missed breakfast (tragic but worth it).

Breakfast: Solid buffet. Enough options to “fuel the adventure” (and then some). I ate like I was sponsored 😅

Photo Spots: Pool, garden, riverside — all very “I swear I travel” vibes 📸

Verdict:
- If you like good views, top location, reasonable prices, and some vintage vibes — this is your spot.
- If you’re 100% modern-minimalism-core… well, Huế will still love you 🥹

Score: 8.5/10 — Would stay again, would eat breakfast again 😂

text:
For years, a Vietnamese bishop locked in a Communist prison said Mass with three drops of wine and one drop of water in the palm of his hand. His name was Francis Xavier Nguyễn Văn Thuận.

He was born on 17 April 1928 in Phú Cam, Huế, Vietnam’s old imperial capital, into a Catholic family. His mother’s brother, Ngô Đình Diệm, later became president of South Vietnam. He entered the An Ninh minor seminary at 13, was ordained a priest on 11 June 1953, and in 1967 was named Bishop of Nha Trang.

In April 1975, days before Saigon fell on 30 April, Pope Paul VI named him coadjutor archbishop of Saigon. The new government saw the appointment, as he later put it, as “proof of a conspiracy between the Vatican and the Imperialists.” On 15 August 1975 he was summoned to the Presidential Palace and arrested.

Held under house arrest near Nha Trang, he asked a young boy to have his mother buy old calendars. Night after night that autumn he wrote short messages to his people on the pages. The boy carried them out to be copied by hand. They became The Road of Hope.

He spent 13 years in detention without trial or sentence, nine in solitary confinement, in places including a Hanoi prison and the Vĩnh Quang re-education camp. Alone, he was tormented by the work he could no longer do, until, he said, a voice in his heart told him to choose God and not the works of God.

His family sent wine in a bottle labeled “medicine for stomach ache,” and hosts were hidden in a flashlight. “Every day, with three drops of wine and a drop of water in the palm of my hand, I celebrated Mass,” he recalled. A guard who became his friend let him saw a small cross from a piece of wood; another brought electric wire for a chain. They became his pectoral cross.

Released on 21 November 1988, he was forced into exile in 1991 and settled in Rome. He led the Pontifical Council for Justice and Peace from 1998, preached the Lenten retreat for John Paul II and the Roman Curia in March 2000 (published as Testimony of Hope), and was made a cardinal on 21 February 2001. He died of cancer in Rome on 16 September 2002. Pope Francis declared him Venerable on 4 May 2017.

In Spe Salvi, Benedict XVI wrote that during his thirteen years in jail, “in a situation of seemingly utter hopelessness, the fact that he could listen and speak to God became for him an increasing power of hope.”

He did not wait for freedom to begin living faithfully. A cell became his cathedral, old calendars his pulpit, and his palm an altar.

“We glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope” (Romans 5:3–4, KJV)

What small act of faith can you still offer in a place you would never have chosen?

Sources: Holy See, biography of Cardinal Nguyễn Văn Thuận; F. X. Nguyễn Văn Thuận, Testimony of Hope, The Road of Hope and Ten Rules of Life; Benedict XVI, Spe Salvi (2007); AsiaNews; Omnes.

text:
Heading to Ho Chi Minh City this November? You might want to keep your evenings free! 🇻🇳🎆

The city is gearing up for a few nights of art, culture, light shows and fireworks, and some of the events are completely free to experience!

📍 November 21–24: 3D projection mapping performances around the HCMC People's Committee headquarters and Rex Hotel. Expect colourful visuals projected onto some of the city's most recognisable buildings.

🎆 November 24, 8 PM: A special cultural programme celebrating Vietnam Culture Day, with an artistic fireworks display planned for the evening.

The programme will connect three locations:
• Nguyen Hue Walking Street, central HCMC
• New City Central Park, Binh Duong Ward
• Tam Thang Tower Square, Vung Tau Ward

If you're visiting Saigon around these dates, this could be a lovely way to spend an evening. 

Save this for your November trip, and keep an eye on official announcements for final timings and event details!

text:
Lance Corporal Daniel Alan Nelson

United States Marine Corps

October 15, 1947 – February 19, 1968

Daniel Alan Nelson, 20, of Detroit, Michigan (Wayne County), was killed during the Battle of Huế in the 1968 Tet Offensive. He served as a rifleman (MOS 0311) with C Company, 1st Battalion, 1st Marines, 1st Marine Division.

Born October 15, 1947, in Michigan, Nelson entered the Marine Corps and began his Vietnam tour on his 20th birthday, October 15, 1967. His unit was committed to the fight for Huế, the old imperial capital in Thừa Thiên Province. The battle ran from 31 January to early March 1968 and was among the longest and costliest urban engagements of the war. Marines, ARVN forces, and supporting units cleared NVA and Viet Cong positions house by house, street by street, inside and around the Citadel. Allied casualties exceeded 600 killed and thousands wounded; the city was heavily damaged and thousands of Vietnamese civilians were killed or executed.

Nelson was wounded by an explosive device (ground casualty) around 9 February 1968. He died of those wounds on 19 February 1968 at the Station Hospital, Naval Support Activity, Da Nang. His remains were recovered. He is honored on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, Panel 40E, Line 27. Records list him as single and Roman Catholic. He was buried at Holy Sepulchre Cemetery in the Detroit area. Awards include the Purple Heart, Combat Action Ribbon, National Defense Service Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, Vietnam Campaign Medal, and unit citations.

A nephew left a remembrance on the Virtual Wall. Public sources contain little further personal detail beyond his service record and the circumstances of his death in the fight for Huế.

text:
Photography, Historical Timelines, and Distorted Identities: Unveiling the Truth Behind "Queen Ang Mey"

In recent years, Cambodian netizens have frequently circulated vintage photographs of high-ranking noblewomen taken by Western photographers in an effort to assert historical claims. Yet, a fundamental examination of nineteenth-century geopolitics reveals that Bangkok was the undisputed political nucleus and premier international trading port in the region. While early daguerreotype experiments were conducted by European colonial authorities in colonized territories such as the Philippines, Indonesia, and Singapore for exploratory purposes, Siam stands as the first sovereign state in Southeast Asia where the ruling monarch deliberately employed photography as an instrument of statecraft and international diplomacy.

This historic milestone is exemplified by the mid-1850s official portraiture of King Mongkut (Rama IV) and Queen Debsirindra, taken alongside their royal regalia and formally dispatched as state gifts to President Franklin Pierce of the United States and Queen Victoria of the United Kingdom. These archival pieces constitute the very first diplomatic photographs of a sovereign Southeast Asian head of state ever presented to the international community, projecting Siam’s sovereignty, civilization, and preeminence as the suzerain power over neighboring vassal states. In stark contrast, viral side-by-side comparisons across social media and TikTok styling themselves as "Cambodian Queen vs. Vietnamese Empress" reflect a gross misrepresentation spanning political history, photographic science, and fabricated historical identity.

The figure on the left, widely mislabeled across Wikipedia entries and TikTok posts as "Queen Ang Mey" (or Somdet Phra Maha Kasattri An Mei), collapses under both primary-source scrutiny and technological reality. Primary court annals from the Nguyễn dynasty of Vietnam—specifically the Đại Nam thực lục (大南寔錄)—alongside modern historiography by Southeast Asian scholar David Chandler (A History of Cambodia), document that Emperor Minh Mạng systematically annexed Cambodia into the Vietnamese commandery of Trấn Tây Thành (鎭西城) under the absolute rule of General Trương Minh Giảng. In June 1840, Vietnamese authorities stripped Ang Mey of her authority and downgraded her status to Mỹ Lâm quận chúa (美林郡主), equivalent to a mere district-level governor, before subsequently detaining and exiling her to Saigon and Huế. She was never a sovereign "Queen Regnant" in any true constitutional or geopolitical sense, but rather a nominal figurehead tightly controlled by the Vietnamese court.

Crucially, during her nominal tenure (1834–1840), daguerreotype photography had only just been patented in France (1839) and had not yet arrived in Indochina, rendering the physical existence of any photographic portrait of her a scientific impossibility. Official French colonial records at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer (ANOM) authenticate the woman in the photograph as Neak Neang Pen (Samdach Preah Voreak Reachani Pen), the principal consort of King Ang Duong and the royal mother of King Norodom I, captured by French pioneer photographer Émile Gsell between 1866 and 1873. By contrast, the figure on the right depicts Empress Nam Phương of Vietnam on her wedding day in 1934—a chronological disparity exceeding six decades.

The supreme historical irony of this viral meme lies in co-opting Neak Neang Pen’s archival image as "indigenous Cambodian heritage" to compete visually with the Imperial Court of Huế. During the actual reign of Queen Ang Mey, imperial Vietnam implemented sweeping Vietnamization decrees, explicitly outlawing the wrapped chong kraben garment and cropped hairstyles, and mandating that Cambodians grow their hair long and adopt Vietnamese-style áo dài tunics and trousers.

Yet, the archival image of Neak Neang Pen showcases the courtly etiquette of the Early Rattanakosin era in meticulous detail: the pom peek (winged crop) hairstyle, the wrapped chong kraben, the pleated sabai draped diagonally, and courtly regalia on the side table—including traditional pedestaled tiered trays (phan waen fah), footed water basins, and Siamese teapots—all of which represent the court craft of Bangkok’s royal artisans. This cultural continuity was the direct legacy of King Ang Duong, who resided in Bangkok for decades before ascending the throne and systematically revived the royal court of Phnom Penh by adopting Siamese court protocols, master craftsmen, language, and royal attire. Rebranding this image online as "Queen Ang Mey" does not simply forge a revisionist past; it appropriates the visual culture, craftsmanship, and regal heritage of the Siamese Royal Court—the very suzerain power that sheltered and reconstituted the Cambodian court—and projects it as an indigenous identity in direct contradiction to historical reality.

References:
 ▪️Đại Nam thực lục (大南寔錄 - Veritable Records of the Great South): Primary court annals of the Nguyễn dynasty, recording the imperial annexation of Cambodia into Trấn Tây Thành and the June 1840 imperial decree demoting Ang Mey (Ngọc Vân) to Mỹ Lâm quận chúa.
 ▪️Chandler, David P. (2008). A History of Cambodia (4th ed.). Westview Press: Documentation on Vietnam’s assimilation policies (Vietnamization) during the 1830s–1840s and the restoration of Cambodian court protocols modeled after the Siamese court under King Ang Duong.   
 ▪️Archives nationales d'outre-mer (ANOM) & Émile Gsell Photographic Collection (c. 1866–1873): French colonial archives authenticating the sitter as Neak Neang Pen, royal mother of King Norodom I.   
 ▪️National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution (Washington, D.C.): Archival record of the 1856 daguerreotype portrait of King Mongkut (Rama IV) and Queen Debsirindra, presented to U.S. President Franklin Pierce.

text:
The Puppet, The Patron, and The Pariah: Deconstructing the Myth of Nineteenth-Century Cambodian Sovereignty (1594–1840)

Modern ultranationalist revisionism in Phnom Penh routinely manufactures a self-serving historical myth: whitewashing centuries of Siamese tributary suzerainty by asserting that nineteenth-century Cambodia was an autonomous kingdom under Vietnamese dominance, while recasting French colonial gunboat diplomacy as voluntary liberation.

Archival records from Hue, Bangkok, and Paris completely destroy this narrative. Primary documentation—specifically the imperial records of the Nguyen dynasty (Đại Nam Thực Lục), the diplomatic archives of Siam, and the records of the French Ministry of Marine and Colonies preserved in the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)—exposes an unbroken continuum of dynastic instability, strategic duplicity, and deep colonial humiliation.

The Historical Genesis: The Fall of Lovek (1594) and the Cycle of Incurable Vulnerability

The political subservience of the post-Angkorian Cambodian polity did not begin in the nineteenth century; its structural collapse was cemented centuries earlier in the ashes of the Siamese-Cambodian wars of the late sixteenth century. Throughout the Ayutthaya-Burmese wars, the Khmer court repeatedly exploited Siamese vulnerabilities by raiding border settlements and taking captives. In response to this persistent treachery, King Naresuan the Great of Ayutthaya mounted a decisive retaliatory expedition, culminating in the Fall of Lovek in January 1594.

As documented by historian David P. Chandler in A History of Cambodia, the sack of Lovek shattered the psychological and political core of the Khmer state. The royal court was forced into perpetual flight, abandoning one provisional capital after another—relocating to Srei Santhor, Koh Sotin, and eventually settling in Udong in 1618—in a desperate effort to escape Siamese military dominance and the inexorable southward expansion of Vietnam (Nam tiến).

Yet, physical relocation could not compensate for internal decay. Crippled by endemic factionalism and dynastic incompetence, Cambodia’s ruling elite proved utterly incapable of sustaining independent sovereignty. Instead of building national cohesion, rival princes institutionalized a disastrous pattern: invoking the armies of the Court of Hue to seize the throne, realizing in horror that Hue’s ultimate agenda was the total eradication of Khmer culture and territorial absorption, running back to Bangkok on bended knees begging for military salvation, and promptly betraying Siam the moment external danger subsided.

1809–1834: Fratricidal Ambition and the Latin Reality of Dual-Vassalage

The crisis of the nineteenth century was the direct culmination of this incurable cycle. Following the death of King Ang Eng in 1796, his four sons—Ang Chan, Ang Snguon, Ang Em, and Ang Duong—plunged the realm into vicious fratricidal civil war, reducing their kingdom to a geopolitical pawn through a calculated policy of playing Siam and Vietnam against one another.

When the eldest son, King Ang Chan II (r. 1806–1834), ascended the throne under Siamese investiture, he swiftly betrayed Bangkok. In 1809, he refused to attend the royal cremation of King Rama I and actively sought military protection from Emperor Gia Long of Vietnam. In response, his alienated brothers—Ang Snguon, Ang Em, and Ang Duong—fled to Bangkok, begging Siam for troops and arms to overthrow their brother.

This entrenched an infamous strategy of duplicitous dual-vassalage—operating strictly under the Roman maxim of altera manu fert lapidem, panem ostentat altera (offering bread with one hand while holding a stone in the other)—calculated to play both regional empires against each other:

▪️The Pro-Hue Faction (Ang Chan): Ang Chan invited Vietnamese garrisons into Phnom Penh, allowing Vietnamese mandarins to construct fortresses and dictate foreign policy, simply to protect his precarious throne from his own brothers.

text:
From the perspective of political history and material archaeology, the collapse of the Angkorian center following protracted conflict with Ayutthaya inaugurated the Post-Angkorian era—a period marked by the structural disintegration of classical imperial hegemony. To escape persistent military incursions from Ayutthaya and an expanding Vietnam, the Cambodian court repeatedly relocated its royal seat southward—moving from Angkor to Chaktomuk, Longvek, Oudong, and eventually Phnom Penh. Yet, this geographical flight could not insulate the realm from external domination. Cambodia was inexorably subsumed into the geopolitical crosscurrents of its two powerful neighbors, degenerating into a factional battleground.

The domestic politics of the Cambodian royal family reflected this structural vulnerability: dynastic rivalries consistently led opposing princely factions to solicit external intervention. Whenever one royal faction faced defeat or political marginalization, it sought military shelter and patronage in Huế, offering territorial concessions or vassalage in exchange for Vietnamese backing. Conversely, rival contenders hastened to Bangkok to pledge fealty to the Siamese court, soliciting troops and political investiture to reclaim the throne. As David Chandler observes, this dynamic rendered the Khmer polity a contested domain where "sovereignty was shared, contested, and continually eroded" (Chandler, 2008, p. 139). This cyclical proxy warfare culminated in the protracted Siam-Vietnamese War of 1841–1845 (the Anam-Siam Yuth), a devastating fourteen-year conflict fought on Cambodian soil that concluded with a negotiated condominium: Siam firmly installed and consecrated King Ang Duong upon the throne under Bangkok's paramount administrative tutelage, while Cambodia was simultaneously bound by treaty to remit triennial tribute—most notably the gold and silver flower trees (bunga mas)—to the court of Huế (Woodside, 1971; Chandler, 2008).

During this subsequent era of stability under early Rattanakosin suzerainty, the court at Bangkok exercised decisive hegemony over the reconstruction, institutional patronage, and ceremonial codification of the Cambodian monarchy. This tributary tutelage extended beyond administrative protocol, royal lexicons, and the performing arts (lakhon luang) to dictate elite sartorial norms. Court garments—most notably the drawn hip-wrapper (chong kraben), pleated breast-cloths (pha thaep), and embroidered shoulder mantles (sbai sapak)—were direct adoptions of stylistic standards institutionalized in Bangkok. Documenting this comprehensive courtly transmission, Jean Moura, the French Representative to Cambodia, noted during the reign of King Norodom:

"The costume of the court, the dances, and the court usages differ in no way from those of Siam... the ladies of the palace drape themselves in long silks, following the fashions and manners imported from Bangkok." (Moura, 1883, Vol. 1, p. 415)

Colonial administrator and linguist Étienne Aymonier corroborated this assessment in Le Cambodge, observing that "the high Cambodian society has adopted the costume, the language of the court, and the customs of Siam to such a degree that it is an exact reflection of Bangkok" (Aymonier, 1900, Vol. 1, p. 57). Consequently, the Cambodian monarchy’s eventual capitulation to French protectorate status under the 1863 treaty represented an instrumental diplomatic realignment: an effort to leverage Western imperial power to break free from Siamese suzerainty and forestall Vietnamese demographic absorption.

Accordingly, recent attempts within Cambodian nationalist historiography to trace an unbroken genealogy connecting modern court attire—specifically the pleated and embroidered sbai—directly to the bas-reliefs of Angkor lack empirical grounding in both primary textual sources and the archaeological record. Epigraphic and sculptural evidence from the Angkorian period predominantly portrays deified Hindu-Buddhist personages, ascetics, and celestial figures whose bare-chested presentation conformed to tropical climatic realities and sacred iconographic convention. The fifteenth-century abandonment of Angkor precipitated a multi-century historical rupture characterized by sweeping socio-religious transformations, leaving no intermediate material record to bridge classical epigraphic drapery with modern royal regalia—a cultural discontinuity systematically demonstrated by Bernard-Philippe Groslier (1958).

Deconstructing this anachronistic formulation, Penny Edwards demonstrates how the colonial apparatus actively engineered an "Angkor-centric" paradigm designed to suppress intermediary history:

"In the colonial imagination, and later in Cambodian nationalism, the centuries of Siamese and Vietnamese suzerainty were treated as an aberration or erased altogether, forging an unmediated link between the glories of Angkor and contemporary royal identity." (Edwards, 2007, p. 38)

By excising documented eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Siamese provenance from Cambodian court regalia and retroactively projecting these garments onto classical Khmer antiquity, contemporary revisionist narratives function as exercises in nationalist myth-making rather than evidence-based historical reconstructions.

text:
Before Hue became known for the Battle of Hue, one of the fiercest battles of the Vietnam War, it was Vietnam’s imperial capital until 1945. The 1968 battle, fought during the Tet Offensive, left much of the historic city devastated.

Centuries earlier, the region was part of the Linyi Kingdom (2nd–4th century CE), with Kandarpapura as its capital, about 3 km from present-day Hue. Kandarpapura means "the city where Siva burned Kama." Linyi became Indianized through the influence of monks and merchants who brought Indian culture, religious traditions, and ideas to the region.
